Cookies.Chocolate chip: The chocolate chip cookie was invented in the 1930s by Ruth Wakefield at the Toll House Inn in Massachusetts. Nestlé later bought her recipe for chips.
Cookies.Snickerdoodle: Snickerdoodle is a cinnamon-sugar cookie, and its odd name may come from a German word. Cream of tartar gives it a tangy chew.
Cookies.Oatmeal raisin: Oatmeal raisin cookies often face a dislike from chocolate lovers. Oats were once promoted as a health food, so these cookies started out as the sensible choice.
Cookies.Shortbread: Shortbread is a Scottish classic of butter, sugar, and flour. Short here means crumbly, because the high butter content stops gluten from forming.
Cookies.Gingersnap: Gingersnaps are spiced cookies that crack on top and snap when bitten. They were popular in early America, and molasses gives them a deep flavor.
Cookies.Biscotti: Biscotti means twice-cooked in Italian, since the loaf is baked, sliced, and baked again. That makes them dry enough to dunk in vin santo.
Cookies.Oreo: Oreo has been sold since 1912 and is billed as the best-selling cookie in the world. The pattern on each cookie has been changed only a few times.
Cookies.Fig Newton: Fig Newtons are named after the town of Newton, Massachusetts, not the physicist. Cookie makers there began them around 1891 to carry fig jam in pastry.
Cookies.Amaretti: Amaretti are Italian almond cookies, whose name means little bitter ones. Traditional recipes use bitter almonds or apricot kernels for the flavor.
Cookies.Speculoos: Speculoos is a spiced Belgian and Dutch cookie traditionally baked for St Nicholas Day. Its paste, sold as Biscoff spread, became a worldwide craze.
Cookies.Anzac biscuit: Anzac biscuits are oat and coconut cookies whose recipe, tradition says, was sent to troops in World War I. Their ingredients kept well over long sea voyages.
Cookies.Florentine: The Florentine is a lacy cookie of nuts and candied fruit, usually backed with chocolate. Despite the name, it likely first appeared in France, not Florence.
Cookies.Scone: A scone is a quick bread, not a cookie, and it is split and topped with jam and cream. In Britain, the pronunciation of scone is a long-running argument.
Cookies.Muffin: A muffin is a quick bread, not a cookie. In Britain, the muffin is a flat yeast bread, while the cupcake-like kind is mainly American.
Cookies.Cupcake: A cupcake is a small cake, not a cookie. The name may come from the cups used to measure ingredients, with the first recipe dating to 1796.
Cookies.Éclair: An éclair is a cream-filled choux pastry, not a cookie. The French name means flash of lightning, probably because it is eaten so quickly.
Cookies.Madeleine: Madeleines are French sponge cakes baked in shell molds, not cookies. Marcel Proust's memory of dipping one in tea launched a famous novel.
Cookies.Doughnut: A doughnut is fried dough, not a baked cookie. One legend says the hole was invented by a sea captain, though the true origin remains unclear.
Cookies.Croissant: A croissant is laminated pastry, not a cookie. It descends from the Austrian kipferl, and French bakers adopted it in the 1800s.
Cookies.Pretzel: A pretzel is a baked bread with a lye bath, not a cookie. Its knotted shape may be linked to monks giving them as rewards to children.
Cookies.Crumpet: A crumpet is a yeast pancake-like cake with holes on top, not a cookie. The holes soak up melted butter, which is the whole point.
Cookies.Profiterole: A profiterole is a choux pastry puff, not a cookie. A pile of them, with chocolate sauce, is the classic French dessert croquembouche.
Cookies.Churro: A churro is fried dough with ridges, not a baked cookie. In Spain they are often dunked in thick hot chocolate for breakfast.
Cookies.Danish: A Danish is a laminated pastry, not a cookie. In Denmark, it is called wienerbrød, which means Vienna bread, tracing its roots to Austrian bakers.

Countries on the equator.Ecuador: Named for the equator itself, the country has a monument near Quito marking the line. The real line lies a few hundred feet away, as GPS later revealed.
Countries on the equator.Colombia: The equator only clips a thin southern slice of Colombia, near the Amazon basin. Most of the country, including Bogotá, lies north of the line.
Countries on the equator.Brazil: The equator crosses northern Brazil near the mouth of the Amazon, passing through the city of Macapá, which has a stadium built to straddle the line.
Countries on the equator.Gabon: The equator cuts across Gabon, which sits on the Atlantic coast of central Africa. Its name comes from a Portuguese word for a hooded cloak.
Countries on the equator.DR Congo: The line crosses the middle of the Congo basin, not far from the city of Mbandaka, so the country spans both hemispheres, with rain nearly every day.
Countries on the equator.Uganda: The equator passes right through Uganda, including near Kampala. Roadside markers there pull in tourists to step between hemispheres.
Countries on the equator.Kenya: The equator crosses central Kenya, and the town of Nanyuki sits on it. Mount Kenya is nearly on the line, yet it still holds glaciers.
Countries on the equator.Somalia: The equator runs through southern Somalia near the Indian Ocean coast, close to Kismayo. Somalia has Africa's longest mainland coastline.
Countries on the equator.Indonesia: The equator passes through Sumatra, Borneo and Sulawesi. Pontianak, on Borneo, sits so close that it celebrates equinox shadow events.
Countries on the equator.Maldives: The equator slips between the southern atolls, in the channel separating Huvadhu from Addu. It's also the flattest country, averaging barely 1.5 m above the sea.
Countries on the equator.Kiribati: Its islands spread across the equator and the 180th meridian. The date line bends around them so the whole nation shares one day.
Countries on the equator.Peru: It lies just south of the equator, so it misses the line. Its northern border with Ecuador is close, but all of Peru is in the southern half.
Countries on the equator.Venezuela: Venezuela stays north of the equator, with its southern tip about a degree short of the line. The equator is just beyond its border in Colombia and Brazil.
Countries on the equator.Nigeria: Nigeria is entirely north of the equator, between about 4 and 14 degrees north. That's why its climate is tropical, with a long dry season in the north.
Countries on the equator.Cameroon: It sits fully north of the equator, with its southern tip about 2 degrees north. Gabon and Congo lie across the line to its south.
Countries on the equator.Tanzania: It is south of the equator by about 1 degree, and its northern tip near Lake Victoria misses the line. Kilimanjaro lies about 3 degrees south.
Countries on the equator.Ethiopia: Ethiopia's southern tip reaches about 3 degrees north, so it misses the line. Kenya lies between it and the equator.
Countries on the equator.Malaysia: It lies between about 1 and 7 degrees north. Its southern tip comes within a few degrees of the line, but doesn't cross it.
Countries on the equator.Singapore: Singapore is just 1 degree north of the equator, close but not on it. Its climate is hot and humid year-round with no real seasons.
Countries on the equator.Sri Lanka: It lies between 5 and 10 degrees north, so it's well clear of the equator. The line passes far south, across the Indian Ocean.
Countries on the equator.Philippines: The Philippines sits entirely north of the equator, between about 5 and 21 degrees north, so it misses the line by a wide margin.
Countries on the equator.Papua New Guinea: The country sits just south of the line, and its Manus Island is about 2 degrees south. Mountain New Guinea hosts over 800 languages.
Countries on the equator.Panama: Panama is about 7 to 9 degrees north, so it's well clear of the equator. It's where the Atlantic and Pacific are connected by the famous canal.
Countries on the equator.Ghana: Ghana is about 5 degrees north. Ocean waters at 0 degrees latitude and longitude, nicknamed Null Island, lie in the Gulf of Guinea just south of the coast.

Places to see wild penguins.Antarctica: Emperor penguins breed here on sea ice in winter, with males incubating a single egg on their feet for about two months in the dark.
Places to see wild penguins.South Africa: At Boulders Beach near Cape Town, African penguins waddle among sunbathers, and they are known as jackass penguins for their donkey-like bray.
Places to see wild penguins.Australia: Little penguins, the smallest species at about 33 cm, parade ashore at dusk on Phillip Island near Melbourne.
Places to see wild penguins.New Zealand: The rare yellow-eyed penguin, or hoiho, nests along the southeast coast and is one of the world's rarest penguins.
Places to see wild penguins.Argentina: Punta Tombo has the largest Magellanic penguin colony outside of Antarctica, with hundreds of thousands of birds.
Places to see wild penguins.Chile: Humboldt and Magellanic penguins both nest on its coast, and Magdalena Island near Punta Arenas is the best known colony.
Places to see wild penguins.Galápagos: The Galápagos penguin is the only penguin that lives right on the equator, kept cool by the Humboldt Current.
Places to see wild penguins.Falkland Islands: Five penguin species breed here, including the gentoo, rockhopper, king and Magellanic, with more than a million birds in total.
Places to see wild penguins.Namibia: A small number of African penguins live on offshore islands along its Atlantic coast, which are part of the cold Benguela Current.
Places to see wild penguins.Peru: Humboldt penguins nest along the dry Pacific coast, and they take their name from the cold current offshore.
Places to see wild penguins.South Georgia: A king penguin colony at St Andrews Bay has been counted at hundreds of thousands of birds, one of the largest in the world.
Places to see wild penguins.Arctic: Penguins live only in the Southern Hemisphere; polar bears and puffins are the Arctic's counterparts, and they never meet.
Places to see wild penguins.Alaska: Puffins and auks fill a similar niche in Alaska, but no wild penguins have ever lived there.
Places to see wild penguins.Greenland: The big flightless bird there was the great auk, a northern 'penguin' that is now extinct; true penguins stay south.
Places to see wild penguins.Iceland: The word penguin may have first described the great auk of the North Atlantic, yet real penguins have never lived in Iceland.
Places to see wild penguins.Norway: Norwegians claim Bouvet Island in the south Atlantic, which has penguins, but mainland Norway has none.
Places to see wild penguins.Canada: Canada has no wild penguins; the birds you may see on its ice are puffins and murres, not penguins.
Places to see wild penguins.Siberia: Wild penguins are found nowhere in Russia, because they live only in the Southern Hemisphere.
Places to see wild penguins.North Pole: The North Pole has no penguins, a common mix-up, because they live in the south and polar bears live in the north.
Places to see wild penguins.Svalbard: The Arctic archipelago has polar bears and walruses but no penguins; those are found only far to the south.
Places to see wild penguins.Scotland: Scotland has no wild penguins, though Edinburgh Zoo's penguin parade is famous and the Antarctic king penguin Sir Nils Olav was knighted there.
Places to see wild penguins.Hawaii: No wild penguins live in Hawaii, although it has monk seals and seabirds, and the warm waters are too far north.
Places to see wild penguins.Japan: Penguins appear in many Japanese aquariums but not in the wild, and the closest relatives there are auklets.
Places to see wild penguins.Lapland: Reindeer, not penguins, live in Lapland, which sits in the far north of Europe and has no wild penguins.

Metric (SI) prefixes.Kilo: Means thousand and comes from Greek chilioi; a kilogram was defined by a metal cylinder in France until 2019.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Mega: Means million, from the Greek for great; a megabyte, meanwhile, was long ambiguous between 1,000,000 and 1,048,576 bytes.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Giga: Means billion, from Greek for giant, as in gigabytes of storage or gigawatts of power.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Tera: Means trillion, from Greek for monster, and it's now the usual size of laptop drives.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Milli: Means one thousandth, from Latin mille; a millimeter is about the thickness of a credit card.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Micro: Means one millionth, from Greek for small; a human hair is about 70 micrometers wide.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Nano: Means one billionth, from Greek for dwarf; a nanometer is about the width of ten atoms in a row.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Pico: Means one trillionth, as in picoseconds; light travels only about 0.3 mm in a picosecond.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Centi: Means one hundredth, from Latin; it's why centimeters and centuries are related to a hundred.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Deci: Means one tenth, from Latin, and is the rare prefix: decibels and deciliters use it.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Peta: Means a quadrillion, 10 to the 15th; Google and Facebook each process petabytes of data daily.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Femto: Means 10 to the minus 15, from Danish for fifteen; femtosecond lasers can capture chemical reactions in action.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Hecto: Means hundred, and is why a hectare is 100 ares; weather maps use hectopascals for pressure.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Mini: A trap: a common prefix meaning small, but it is not an official SI prefix, and nobody uses minimeters in science.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Ultra: A trap: it means beyond in Latin, as in ultraviolet, yet it is not part of the SI system.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Hyper: A trap: it means over or excess in Greek; it is not a metric prefix, though the opposite of hypo.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Super: A trap: meaning above, a common English prefix, but the metric system doesn't have super as one.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Semi: A trap: meaning half, as in semicircle; there is no semimeter in SI, though.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Multi: A trap: just means many; SI prefixes denote exact powers of ten, which multi does not.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Poly: A trap: Greek for many, as in polygon, so not a metric prefix.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Quasi: A trap: Latin for as if, used in words like quasar; it has no SI value.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Penta: A trap: Greek for five, as in pentagon, so it is not an SI prefix, though SI does use peta, which sounds similar.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Tetra: A trap: Greek for four; tera, with one fewer letter, is the SI one, and the names are related.
Metric (SI) prefixes.Hexa: A trap: Greek for six, as in hexagon; there is no SI prefix for six.

Cave formations.Stalactite: Hangs from the ceiling and grows from mineral-rich dripping water. They grow slowly, often just a centimeter in a century.
Cave formations.Stalagmite: Rises from the floor where dripping water lands. A common memory trick is that stalactites hold tight to the ceiling.
Cave formations.Flowstone: A sheet of mineral deposit formed by water flowing over cave walls or floors. It often looks like frozen waterfalls.
Cave formations.Helictite: A twisting cave formation that grows in odd directions, defying gravity. Scientists still debate how capillary forces and crystal growth create them.
Cave formations.Cave pearl: A small, round ball of calcite formed in a shallow pool when a grain of sand is rolled by dripping water. They really can look like pearls.
Cave formations.Soda straw: A hollow, thin stalactite with a width of a drinking straw. Water drips through the middle, and they can grow very long and fragile.
Cave formations.Cave bacon: A banded sheet of calcite that hangs like strips of bacon. Impurities in the water give the stripes of brown and red.
Cave formations.Rimstone: Natural dams of calcite that form around pools in caves, also called gours. They can create terraced pools like staircases.
Cave formations.Moonmilk: A soft, creamy white deposit in caves, formed partly by microbes. It was once believed to have healing powers.
Cave formations.Geode: A hollow rock lined with crystals, but it forms inside rock, not as a cave formation. Cut open, many are spectacular.
Cave formations.Geyser: A hot spring that erupts with steam and water, found in volcanic areas. Old Faithful erupts about every 90 minutes.
Cave formations.Fossil: The preserved remains of ancient life. Fossils may turn up in caves, but they aren't formed by cave processes.
Cave formations.Meteorite: A rock from space that has fallen to Earth. It's not something caves make.
Cave formations.Sand dune: A wind-blown ridge of sand found in deserts and beaches. Singing dunes can even hum, but they aren't in caves.
Cave formations.Glacier: A slow river of ice. Ice caves can form inside glaciers, but the glacier isn't a cave formation.
Cave formations.Iceberg: A piece of ice broken off a glacier. About nine-tenths of an iceberg sits below the water.
Cave formations.Fjord: A deep sea inlet carved by a glacier. Norway's coast is famous for them.
Cave formations.River delta: Land built from river sediment at the mouth. The Nile delta is so fertile that it supported ancient Egypt.
Cave formations.Mesa: A flat-topped hill with steep sides, from Spanish for table. It's shaped by erosion above ground.
Cave formations.Butte: A smaller, steep-sided hill with a flat top, narrower than a mesa. Monument Valley is full of them.
Cave formations.Atoll: A ring-shaped coral reef around a lagoon. Darwin proposed that they form on sinking volcanic islands.
Cave formations.Hoodoo: A tall, thin spire of rock sculpted by erosion. Bryce Canyon is full of them, but they form in the open.
Cave formations.Sea arch: A natural arch carved by waves in a coastal cliff. They eventually collapse into sea stacks.
Cave formations.Crater: A bowl made by an impact or volcanic explosion. It's an open-air feature, not a cave one.

Super Mario characters.Rosalina: A guardian of the cosmos who debuted in Super Mario Galaxy in 2007, with her Lumas as stars.
Super Mario characters.Koopa Troopa: A walking turtle; stomping one leaves its shell, which can then be kicked as a weapon.

Chess openings.Sicilian Defense: Black's reply of 1...c5 is the most popular response to 1.e4 at the top level and gives asymmetrical play, and it is known for sharp tactics.
Chess openings.Ruy Lopez: The Ruy Lopez, also called the Spanish Game, is named after a 16th-century Spanish priest who analysed it, and it's one of the oldest openings still played.
Chess openings.Queen's Gambit: Despite the name, it's not a real gambit: White's pawn offering on move two can be recaptured, and the 2020 Netflix series made it a household name.
Chess openings.French Defense: The French Defense starts 1.e4 e6, and it is known for a solid, closed structure, but a tricky bishop on c8.
Chess openings.King's Indian: The King's Indian is a hypermodern setup where Black lets White build a big centre, then attacks it, and was a favourite of Fischer and Kasparov.
Chess openings.Caro-Kann: The Caro-Kann is a solid reply to 1.e4 with 1...c6, named after Horatio Caro and Marcus Kann, who analysed it in the 1880s.
Chess openings.Italian Game: One of the oldest openings, it aims at the f7 square and has been played since the 16th century.
Chess openings.English Opening: The English Opening, 1.c4, is named after English player Howard Staunton, who used it in the 1843 match against Saint-Amant.
Chess openings.Scandinavian: The Scandinavian, 1...d5 against 1.e4, is one of the oldest recorded openings, mentioned in a 15th-century manuscript.
Chess openings.London System: The London System is a solid setup for White that can be used against nearly everything, and it's popular with club players.
Chess openings.Dutch Defense: The Dutch Defense is Black's aggressive 1...f5 reply to 1.d4, and it is the favourite of some attacking players.
Chess openings.Pirc Defense: The Pirc Defense is a flexible, hypermodern defence named after Slovenian grandmaster Vasja Pirc.
Chess openings.Hail Mary: A Hail Mary is a desperate long pass in American football, not a chess opening.
Chess openings.Pick and roll: The pick and roll is a basketball play where one player blocks a defender, then cuts to the basket.
Chess openings.Full nelson: The full nelson is a wrestling hold, not a chess opening.
Chess openings.Zone defense: Zone defense is a basketball or football strategy, not a chess opening.
Chess openings.Triangle offense: The triangle offense is a basketball system used by the Chicago Bulls and Lakers.
Chess openings.Wishbone: The wishbone is an American football formation with a three-back arrangement.
Chess openings.Power play: A power play is an ice hockey advantage when the other team has a penalty.
Chess openings.Wildcat: The wildcat is a football formation where a running back takes the snap.
Chess openings.Statue of Liberty: The Statue of Liberty is a trick football play, where the quarterback fakes a pass and hands off behind.
Chess openings.Fosbury flop: The Fosbury flop is Dick Fosbury's backward high jump style, which won him the 1968 Olympic gold.
Chess openings.Nutmeg: A nutmeg in soccer is passing the ball through an opponent's legs.
Chess openings.Rope-a-dope: Rope-a-dope was Muhammad Ali's boxing strategy against George Foreman in 1974.

Lawn games.Croquet: Croquet is played by hitting balls through hoops with mallets, and it is surprisingly tactical. It's the sport of the Queen of Hearts in Alice in Wonderland.
Lawn games.Bocce: Players toss balls to get closest to a small ball called the pallino. It's an Italian favorite and thought to descend from ancient Roman games.
Lawn games.Cornhole: Cornhole tosses bean bags at a slanted board with a hole. A bag in the hole earns three points.
Lawn games.Horseshoes: Players pitch horseshoes at a stake, and a ringer scores three points. It's said to descend from Roman soldiers' games.
Lawn games.Ladder toss: Also called ladder golf, you throw bolas, two golf balls tied together, to wrap around the rungs of a ladder.
Lawn games.Kubb: Kubb is a Swedish game with wooden blocks, often called Viking chess. Players topple the king after knocking the other side's blocks down.
Lawn games.Lawn bowls: Bowls are weighted to curve, so players aim toward a jack. The game dates back to at least the 13th century.
Lawn games.Petanque: Pétanque is a French game of throwing metal balls close to the little jack. It originated in 1907 in La Ciotat.
Lawn games.Spikeball: Players hit a ball off a small trampoline net in a 2v2 game, and it exploded in popularity in the 2010s.
Lawn games.Ring toss: Ring toss means throwing rings over a peg, and it's a staple of fairs and gardens.
Lawn games.Washer toss: Players toss metal washers at a box with holes. It's easy to set up and enjoyed at barbecues.
Lawn games.Billiards: Billiards is a table game, played indoors with cues on cloth. Its origin is found in an outdoor game like croquet.
Lawn games.Darts: Darts is a pub game, not a lawn game. A dartboard has 20 numbered sections and a bull.
Lawn games.Table tennis: Ping pong was marketed in the 1900s and moved from drawing rooms to world championships. It's an indoor sport.
Lawn games.Foosball: Foosball is a tabletop soccer game, and it's an indoor game, so not a lawn game.
Lawn games.Air hockey: Air hockey pucks float on air jets, and the game's tables are found in arcades.
Lawn games.Pinball: Pinball machines were banned in many US cities in the mid-1900s. They're arcade machines, not lawn games.
Lawn games.Tenpin bowling: Tenpin bowling is an indoor sport on wooden or synthetic lanes. It's not a lawn game.
Lawn games.Squash: Squash is an indoor racquet game. It's the lawn game's cousin only by being a ball sport.
Lawn games.Racquetball: Racquetball is played in indoor courts, so it doesn't count as a lawn game.
Lawn games.Skee-Ball: Skee-Ball is an arcade game of rolling balls up a ramp into rings, and it was invented in 1908.
Lawn games.Snooker: Snooker is a table cue sport, indoors. It was invented by British army officers in India in the 1870s.
Lawn games.Curling: Curling is played on ice, and it's called chess on ice. Not a lawn game.
Lawn games.Ice hockey: Ice hockey is an ice sport, not a lawn game, though it also uses a stick.

Chinese dynasties.Han: Ruled 206 BC to AD 220 and gave its name to China's majority people, the Han Chinese. It also saw paper invented and the Silk Road open.
Chinese dynasties.Tang: The golden age of poetry, from 618 to 907, whose capital Chang'an may have held a million people. Its art and trade spread across Asia.
Chinese dynasties.Song: Ran 960 to 1279, and saw movable type, gunpowder weapons and paper money. It was a time of astonishing innovation.
Chinese dynasties.Ming: Ruled 1368 to 1644 and built most of the Great Wall that still stands. Its blue-and-white porcelain was famous worldwide.
Chinese dynasties.Qing: China's last dynasty, 1644 to 1912, founded by the Manchu people. Men were required to wear the queue braid.
Chinese dynasties.Qin: It lasted just 15 years, from 221 BC, but unified China, and gave it its name. Its first emperor was buried with a terracotta army.
Chinese dynasties.Zhou: The longest dynasty, lasting from about 1046 to 256 BC. Confucius lived in its later years, and it brought the idea of the "Mandate of Heaven".
Chinese dynasties.Shang: The earliest dynasty with written evidence, c. 1600 to 1046 BC. Its oracle bones are carved with some of the oldest Chinese writing.
Chinese dynasties.Yuan: Founded by Kublai Khan in 1271, it was the Mongol dynasty. Marco Polo supposedly served at Kublai's court.
Chinese dynasties.Sui: A short dynasty, 581 to 618, that reunited China after centuries of division. It built the Grand Canal, an engineering feat.
Chinese dynasties.Edo: The Japanese period from 1603 to 1868 centred on today's Tokyo. Shoguns ruled and Japan was largely closed to the outside world.
Chinese dynasties.Meiji: The Japanese era from 1868, which modernised Japan swiftly. It is named for Emperor Meiji, with the Tokyo palace as its seat.
Chinese dynasties.Tokugawa: The shogun family that ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868. It is a Japanese shogunate, not a Chinese dynasty.
Chinese dynasties.Joseon: The Korean dynasty from 1392 to 1897, which created the Hangul alphabet in the 1440s. It was a long-lived Korean kingdom.
Chinese dynasties.Mughal: A Muslim empire in India, 1526 to 1857. It built the Taj Mahal and its rulers were descended from Timur and Genghis Khan.
Chinese dynasties.Khmer: The Cambodian empire at Angkor. It's Southeast Asian, with its own kings and temples.
Chinese dynasties.Ottoman: The empire that took Constantinople in 1453 and lasted until 1922. It is Turkish and spanned three continents.
Chinese dynasties.Tudor: England's royal house from 1485 to 1603, including Henry VIII and Elizabeth I. It is English, not Chinese.
Chinese dynasties.Habsburg: A major European dynasty centred in Austria. It ruled the Holy Roman Empire and Spain, and had a famous jutting jaw.
Chinese dynasties.Romanov: Russia's imperial family from 1613 until 1917. They ruled for over 300 years, and are European.
Chinese dynasties.Bourbon: The French royal house of Louis XIV, which also ruled Spain. A branch still sits on the Spanish throne.
Chinese dynasties.Plantagenet: England's medieval house from 1154 to 1485. The name came from the sprig of broom (planta genista) worn by an ancestor.
Chinese dynasties.Goryeo: The Korean dynasty from 918 to 1392, from which the word "Korea" derives. It's Korean, not Chinese.
Chinese dynasties.Shogun: A Japanese military ruler, not a dynasty. The title means "general", and shoguns held real power while emperors were figureheads.

Scholars of the Islamic Golden Age.Al-Farabi: A philosopher called 'the Second Teacher' after Aristotle, who wrote on logic, politics and music.

Scholars of the Islamic Golden Age.Confucius: Trap: the Chinese thinker of about 500 BC. He lived in a very different culture and era from the Islamic world.

Scholars of the Islamic Golden Age.Paracelsus: Trap: a Swiss physician of the early 1500s who shook up medicine, a European of a later era.

Things usually made of wood.Popsicle stick: The Popsicle was invented by an 11-year-old, Frank Epperson, who left a drink with a stirring stick outside overnight in 1905.
Things usually made of wood.Violin: Spruce is used for the top and maple for the back, and the wood's age and cut shape the sound.
Things usually made of wood.Cuckoo clock: They come from Germany's Black Forest, and the cuckoo call is made by two small bellows and whistles.
Things usually made of wood.Matchstick: Safety matches were invented in Sweden in the 1850s, which put the flammable part on the box rather than the stick.
Things usually made of wood.Log cabin: Log cabins are thought to have come to North America with Swedish and Finnish settlers in the 1600s.
Things usually made of wood.Wine barrel: Oak barrels give wine vanilla and spice notes, and a barrel is often only used for a few vintages.
Things usually made of wood.Jenga block: Jenga is named after the Swahili word for 'build', and the game was created by a Kenyan-born British designer.

Things usually made of wood.Fork: Forks in everyday life are metal or plastic, and wooden forks are mostly for salads or cooking.

Things usually made of wood.Sock: Socks are knitted from cotton, wool, or synthetic fibers, never wood, though wood-derived viscose is a real fabric.
Things usually made of wood.Kettle: Kettles are metal, plastic, or ceramic, because anything wooden would burn when heated.

Things that keep things warm.Thermos: A vacuum flask works because the vacuum between its walls blocks nearly all heat conduction; James Dewar invented it in 1892.
Things that keep things warm.Tea cozy: Tea cozies became popular in Victorian Britain, when afternoon tea turned a hot pot into a social ritual.
Things that keep things warm.Hot water bottle: Rubber hot water bottles date back to the 1800s, and many hold a gallon or so that stays warm for hours.
Things that keep things warm.Electric blanket: Electric blankets use thin heating wires woven in, and modern ones switch themselves off to avoid overheating.
Things that keep things warm.Heat lamp: Heat lamps are used to keep newborn chicks warm and french fries crisp, two jobs that need steady warmth.
Things that keep things warm.Radiator: Radiators actually warm mostly by convection, pushing hot air up, rather than by radiating heat as their name suggests.
Things that keep things warm.Duvet: A duvet traps body heat in pockets of air; real eiderdown from Icelandic ducks is among the best insulators known.
Things that keep things warm.Insulated mug: Insulated mugs rely on the same double-wall trick as flasks, so your coffee stays hot for hours.
Things that keep things warm.Hand warmer: Many hand warmers work by oxidizing iron powder, which is essentially controlled rusting that gives off heat.
Things that keep things warm.Egg cozy: Egg cozies are a British breakfast tradition, knitted to keep a soft-boiled egg from cooling while you eat toast.
Things that keep things warm.Warming tray: Warming trays keep dishes hot at buffets, usually with a heating element or gel fuel burners called Sternos.
Things that keep things warm.Fridge: A fridge does the opposite job, holding food around 4 degrees Celsius to slow bacteria growth.
Things that keep things warm.Ice pack: Ice packs are meant to keep things cold, usually with gel that freezes around 0 degrees Celsius.
Things that keep things warm.Freezer: A freezer stays near minus 18 Celsius, a standard chosen to halt bacterial growth in food.
Things that keep things warm.Desk fan: A desk fan cools you by speeding evaporation of sweat; it doesn't change the room's actual temperature.
Things that keep things warm.Colander: A colander only drains water; it holds food but doesn't keep anything warm.
Things that keep things warm.Ice cube tray: An ice cube tray is built to cool; Clarence Birdseye's flash freezing method helped make frozen food widespread.
Things that keep things warm.Air conditioner: Air conditioners cool by moving heat outside, and Willis Carrier built the first modern one in 1902 for a printing plant.
Things that keep things warm.Sieve: A sieve filters out clumps or liquid, and doesn't retain heat in any meaningful way.
Things that keep things warm.Paper plate: A paper plate offers almost no insulation, so hot food cools on it about as fast as on the table.
Things that keep things warm.Salad bowl: A salad bowl holds cold greens and has no insulating role, though chilling the bowl keeps the salad crisp.
Things that keep things warm.Wine chiller: A wine chiller keeps bottles cold; white wine is usually best served around 7 to 10 Celsius.
Things that keep things warm.Cooling rack: A cooling rack lets baked goods lose heat quickly by letting air flow underneath, the opposite of warming.
Things that keep things warm.Popsicle mold: A popsicle mold freezes juice into a treat, and the Popsicle was reportedly invented by an 11-year-old in 1905.

Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Live crab: A live crab would pinch you through the fabric, and crabs on the move can use their strong claws to cut right through cloth.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Hot coal: Hot coal in a pocket burns a hole through it fast, and coal can smolder for hours even after it looks dark.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Ice cream: Ice cream in a pocket turns to a sticky mess quickly, and ice cream melts at around minus 5 C once it's out of the freezer.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Soup: Soup in a pocket is a spill waiting to happen, and it's a reminder that pockets are no good for liquids.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Scorpion: A scorpion in a pocket would sting, and while most species are harmless to humans, some produce venom that's dangerous.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Lit candle: A lit candle in a pocket would burn the fabric, and open flame near cloth starts house fires.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Wasp: A wasp in a pocket is a bad idea, since a trapped wasp stings repeatedly when it feels crushed.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Raw egg: A raw egg would crack on the first bump, and raw eggs can carry salmonella, a risk to you and your pocket.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Wet paintbrush: A wet paintbrush leaves a stain through the fabric, and a paint stain can be impossible to remove once it dries.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Gravy: Gravy is a thickened sauce, and in a pocket it would soak through to the skin in moments.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Spaghetti: Spaghetti in a pocket would be a messy gag, and Italians say 'spaghetti' is the plural of 'spaghetto', meaning little string.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Melting popsicle: A melting popsicle drips onto your leg, and on a hot day a popsicle may take only minutes to turn into syrup.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Keys: Keys are the classic pocket item, and keys have jingled in pockets since the lock-and-key was perfected in ancient Egypt.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Wallet: Wallets are traditionally pocket-sized, though doctors warn that a thick back-pocket wallet can irritate the sciatic nerve.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Phone: Phones sit in pockets, and the average pocket-sized smartphone has more computing power than the computers that took Apollo to the moon.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Tissues: Tissues are a pocket staple, and the first disposable tissue was marketed by Kleenex in the 1920s for removing cold cream.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Coins: Coins in a pocket jingle, and the word 'pocket money' goes back centuries to the small amount you carry for treats.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Lip balm: Lip balm is a handy pocket item, but leave it in a hot car and it can melt, so a pocket suits it better.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Pen: A pen in a pocket may leak with altitude changes, and ballpoints are the least likely to burst in a shirt pocket.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Gum: Gum is handy in a pocket, and the chewing gum tradition goes back thousands of years to birch bark tar chewing.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Receipt: A receipt in a pocket often ends up in the laundry, and thermal receipt paper can fade over time, so photographing it is smart.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Earbuds: Earbuds in a pocket tangle themselves, and a study at UC San Diego showed knots form in seconds in a tumbling cord.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Bus pass: A bus pass lives in a pocket, and many transit cards use contactless chips that work through your clothing.
Things you shouldn't keep in your pocket.Hand sanitizer: Hand sanitizer's small bottle fits a pocket, and its alcohol content needs to be about 60 percent to kill germs well.

Things that have a tail.Dog: Dogs wag their tails to communicate, and studies show a wag to the right side signals a happier mood than to the left.
Things that have a tail.Comet: A comet's tail points away from the Sun, no matter which way it's traveling, because it's blown outward by solar wind.
Things that have a tail.Kite: A kite's tail adds drag and steadies it, and without one many kites would spin out of control.
Things that have a tail.Airplane: An airplane's tail, or empennage, keeps it stable, and the vertical fin is what stops it from yawing side to side.
Things that have a tail.Tadpole: A tadpole has a tail it uses to swim, and as it becomes a frog, the tail is absorbed back into its body.
Things that have a tail.Coin: The coin's 'tails' side gets its name from old coins that carried a king's head on one side and not his tail on the other.
Things that have a tail.Mouse: A mouse's tail helps it balance and regulate its temperature, and it can be as long as the body.
Things that have a tail.Kangaroo: A kangaroo's thick tail acts like a fifth leg when it walks slowly, and it props the animal up while resting.
Things that have a tail.Lizard: Many lizards drop their tails to escape predators, and the tail often regrows, though it never looks quite the same.
Things that have a tail.Peacock: A peacock's famous 'tail' is actually long upper tail coverts, and a male can fan it into a display with about 200 feathers.
Things that have a tail.Fox: A fox's bushy tail, called a brush, serves as a warm wrap in cold weather and helps with balance when turning.
Things that have a tail.Horse: A horse's tail swishes away flies, and a horse tail's hair is what traditionally strings violin bows.
Things that have a tail.Human: A trap: humans have no tail, but we have a tailbone, or coccyx, which is what remains of our tailed ancestors.
Things that have a tail.Gorilla: Gorillas are apes, and apes have no tails, which is one of the main features that separates them from monkeys.
Things that have a tail.Chimpanzee: Chimpanzees are tailless apes, and their close genetic relation to us is about 98 percent in DNA.
Things that have a tail.Frog: A frog has no tail as an adult, but it did as a tadpole, and its tail is absorbed during metamorphosis.
Things that have a tail.Toad: Toads, like frogs, lose their tails when they mature from tadpoles into land-dwelling adults.
Things that have a tail.Spider: Spiders have no tail, though a scorpion does, so a quick look at the rear end can sort arachnids out.
Things that have a tail.Starfish: Starfish have arms rather than a tail, and the five-armed body plan is a form of radial symmetry.
Things that have a tail.Jellyfish: Jellyfish have no tail, and they're about 95 percent water, with no brain, bones, or heart.
Things that have a tail.Orangutan: Orangutans are tailless apes, and their name means 'person of the forest' in Malay.
Things that have a tail.Octopus: An octopus has eight arms and no tail, and it has three hearts and blue blood.
Things that have a tail.Butterfly: A butterfly has no tail in the usual sense, though the swallowtail's wings have tail-like extensions that confuse predators.
Things that have a tail.Bonobo: Bonobos are tailless apes, and they're known for resolving conflict with social behavior instead of fights.

Jobs in a stage theater.Prompter: The prompter sits in the wings with the script to feed actors forgotten lines, a job that used to be common in opera houses.
Jobs in a stage theater.Usher: Ushers show audiences to their seats and hand out programmes, and in many small theatres they're volunteers who love the stage.
Jobs in a stage theater.Stagehand: Stagehands move scenery and props, often in total darkness, and a scene change can happen in seconds without the audience noticing.
Jobs in a stage theater.Understudy: An understudy learns a role in case the lead can't perform, and a famous few have become stars after stepping in on short notice.
Jobs in a stage theater.Set designer: A set designer builds the visual world of the play, and stage sets have to survive hundreds of performances.
Jobs in a stage theater.Costume designer: Costume designers dress actors for the era and mood, and costumes need to withstand quick changes mid-show.
Jobs in a stage theater.Lighting designer: Lighting designers shape mood and focus with light, and they programme hundreds of cues for a single show.
Jobs in a stage theater.Box office clerk: The box office clerk sells tickets, and in many theatres the box office was historically a small booth by the entrance.
Jobs in a stage theater.Dresser: A dresser helps actors with quick costume changes, sometimes in under a minute, working in the dark wings.
Jobs in a stage theater.Best boy: The best boy is a film job, assisting the gaffer, and has no counterpart in stage theatre under that name.
Jobs in a stage theater.Clapper loader: Clapper loaders work with film cameras and the clapperboard, which has no use on a live stage.
Jobs in a stage theater.Boom operator: Boom operators hold mics over film actors. Stage actors usually wear body mics instead, so there's no pole.
Jobs in a stage theater.Cinematographer: Cinematographers shoot films, and a stage show is lit and seen from a seat, so there's no camera and no cinematographer.
Jobs in a stage theater.Golf caddie: Golf caddies work on a golf course, in the open air, far from the stage.
Jobs in a stage theater.Croupier: Croupiers run casino tables, so they belong in a casino, and not in a theatre.
Jobs in a stage theater.Jockey: Jockeys ride racehorses, and not in a theatre, even though a few have been in stage shows.
Jobs in a stage theater.Bellhop: Bellhops carry bags in hotels. The nearest theatre equivalent might be a stagehand, but a bellhop isn't one.
Jobs in a stage theater.Midwife: Midwives deliver babies, and the only time they'd show up at a theatre is for a very surprising night out.
Jobs in a stage theater.Lumberjack: Lumberjacks cut down trees. Their timber may become stage flats, but they don't work in the theatre.
Jobs in a stage theater.Sommelier: Sommeliers handle wine in restaurants, and many theatre bars sell wine, but they don't need a trained sommelier.
Jobs in a stage theater.Farrier: Farriers shoe horses. A theatre may feature horses in a show, but a farrier is not on the regular staff.
Jobs in a stage theater.Shepherd: Shepherds care for sheep in fields, not on a stage, except when one appears in a nativity play.
Jobs in a stage theater.Bank teller: Bank tellers work in banks, so a theatre needs its box office clerk, not a teller.

Things a surgeon wears.Scrubs: Surgical scrubs are traditionally green or blue because the colors rest eyes after staring at red tissue, and reduce afterimages.
Things a surgeon wears.Surgical mask: Surgical masks were first worn in the 1890s, and are designed mainly to stop the wearer's droplets from reaching an open wound.
Things a surgeon wears.Latex gloves: Rubber gloves came into surgery in 1890 when William Halsted had them made for his nurse, whose hands were irritated by antiseptics.
Things a surgeon wears.Surgical gown: Surgical gowns are made to resist fluids, and are sterile on the front, so surgeons keep their hands in front of the chest.
Things a surgeon wears.Surgical cap: Caps keep hair and skin flakes off the sterile field, and many surgeons choose fun patterned ones, which are allowed if laundered.
Things a surgeon wears.Shoe covers: Shoe covers keep blood and fluids off a surgeon's shoes, and keep dirt from the street out of the operating room.
Things a surgeon wears.Face shield: A face shield protects against splashes of blood, and is worn over a mask during procedures where fluids spray.
Things a surgeon wears.Loupes: Loupes are small binocular magnifiers mounted on glasses, letting surgeons see fine detail, and they're custom fit to the surgeon's working distance.
Things a surgeon wears.Clogs: Many surgeons wear washable clogs because they're comfortable for long operations, wipe clean, and are easy to disinfect.
Things a surgeon wears.Hard hat: A hard hat protects a construction worker's head from falling objects, and isn't part of the operating room's sterile dress.
Things a surgeon wears.Hi-vis vest: High-visibility vests are worn by road crews and cyclists to be seen, while operating rooms need no help seeing the surgeon.
Things a surgeon wears.Toque: A toque is the tall white chef's hat. Legend says its 100 pleats stand for the ways a chef can cook an egg.
Things a surgeon wears.Spurs: Spurs are worn on a rider's boots to cue a horse, and are a poor choice around an operating table.
Things a surgeon wears.Chaps: Chaps are leather leg guards for cowboys riding through brush, and nothing a surgeon would wear.
Things a surgeon wears.Waders: Waders are waterproof overalls for fishing, and surgeons stay dry without them.
Things a surgeon wears.Turnout coat: A firefighter's turnout coat has layers of flame-resistant fabric, and is made for fire, not the operating room.
Things a surgeon wears.Tool belt: A tool belt holds a carpenter's or electrician's tools, and a surgeon's instruments sit on a sterile tray instead.
Things a surgeon wears.Bowler hat: The bowler hat was designed in 1849 in London as a hard hat for gamekeepers, and later became a symbol of city gents.
Things a surgeon wears.Snorkel: A snorkel is a breathing tube for swimmers. A surgeon does fine on the air in the operating room.
Things a surgeon wears.Kilt: The kilt is traditional Scottish dress, and not what you want in a sterile operating theater.
Things a surgeon wears.Tiara: A tiara is a jeweled crown for royalty and pageant winners, and the operating room is no place for sparkling gems.
Things a surgeon wears.Cowboy boots: The high heel on cowboy boots keeps the foot from slipping through a stirrup, which is useless in surgery.
Things a surgeon wears.Chain mail: Chain mail is armor made of interlocking metal rings, and butchers do wear mail gloves, but surgeons don't.
Things a surgeon wears.Top hat: Top hats were fashionable gentlemen's wear in the 1800s, and an unsterile choice for a surgeon.

Titles ending in 'General'.Attorney General: In the U.S. the attorney general leads the Justice Department, and in many British-style systems is the government's chief legal adviser.
Titles ending in 'General'.Surgeon General: The U.S. Surgeon General is called the nation's doctor, and the 1964 report on smoking by one was a landmark in public health.
Titles ending in 'General'.Postmaster General: Benjamin Franklin was the first Postmaster General of the colonies, and the post was a Cabinet job until 1971.
Titles ending in 'General'.Governor-General: A governor-general represents the monarch in a realm such as Canada or Australia, and performs ceremonial duties.
Titles ending in 'General'.Inspector General: Inspectors general audit agencies for waste and fraud, and the U.S. has dozens of them in government departments.
Titles ending in 'General'.Secretary-General: The United Nations has a Secretary-General, and the first, Trygve Lie of Norway, took office in 1946.
Titles ending in 'General'.Major General: A major general holds two stars and outranks a brigadier general, though oddly a lieutenant general outranks a major general.
Titles ending in 'General'.Brigadier General: A brigadier general is a one-star rank, the lowest of general officers, who in the U.S. commands a brigade.
Titles ending in 'General'.Consul General: A consul general leads a major consulate, which helps citizens abroad with visas and passports, but is not an embassy.
Titles ending in 'General'.Solicitor General: The Solicitor General of the U.S. argues the government's cases before the Supreme Court, and ranks just below the attorney general.
Titles ending in 'General'.General store: The general store sold a bit of everything in small towns, but General here is an adjective, not a title following a noun.
Titles ending in 'General'.General public: General public means ordinary people, with General as an adjective, and so not a title.
Titles ending in 'General'.General election: A general election is a nationwide vote, as opposed to a primary, and general is an adjective here.
Titles ending in 'General'.General admission: General admission tickets have no assigned seat, and general is an adjective.
Titles ending in 'General'.General practice: A general practitioner treats common ailments, and general here means broad.
Titles ending in 'General'.General knowledge: General knowledge is broad facts, which is what pub quizzes test, and general is not a rank.
Titles ending in 'General'.General strike: A general strike halts a whole economy, such as Britain's in 1926, and general here means widespread.
Titles ending in 'General'.General anesthetic: General anesthesia makes a patient unconscious, and it was first publicly shown in Boston in 1846 with ether.
Titles ending in 'General'.General Motors: General Motors began in 1908 as a merger, and General is part of the name, not a rank or title.
Titles ending in 'General'.General manager: A general manager oversees operations, and general means overall rather than a military rank.
Titles ending in 'General'.General relativity: Einstein published general relativity in 1915, and it showed that gravity is the bending of spacetime.
Titles ending in 'General'.General ledger: A general ledger is the main accounting record, and general here means main.
Titles ending in 'General'.General studies: General studies are introductory courses across subjects, with general meaning broad.
Titles ending in 'General'.General Mills: General Mills is a food company known for Cheerios, and its name comes from flour mills, with no army involved.

Things a magician uses.Top hat: Pulling a rabbit from a hat is a stage cliché, and the top hat itself was just a 19th-century gentleman's fashion.
Things a magician uses.Magic wand: A wand is misdirection: the audience follows its tip while the other hand does the real work.
Things a magician uses.Cape: Its swirl is built-in cover, since a quick flourish hides whatever the other hand is doing.
Things a magician uses.Deck of cards: A well-shuffled 52-card deck is almost certainly in an order that has never existed before in history.
Things a magician uses.Rabbit: Producing a rabbit became a magic icon in the 19th century, and conjurers even keep special hidden pockets for it.
Things a magician uses.Silk scarves: Silk squeezes into a tiny ball and slides easily, which makes it ideal for production and vanishing tricks.
Things a magician uses.Cups and balls: Often called magic's oldest trick, it was performed by street conjurers in ancient Rome.
Things a magician uses.Linking rings: Eight solid steel rings seem to link and unlink; one ring has a secret gap that makes it possible.
Things a magician uses.Trick coins: Specially machined coins, some hollow or double-faced, power magical vanishes and transformations.
Things a magician uses.Assistant: P. T. Selbit first sawed a woman in half on stage in 1921, and an assistant has been central to magic since.
Things a magician uses.Lasso: A cowboy's rope; rope tricks exist, but a lasso is a ranch tool, not a typical magic prop.
Things a magician uses.Stethoscope: A doctor's tool, invented in 1816 from a rolled-up paper tube, that has nothing to do with conjuring.
Things a magician uses.Stopwatch: Athletes and coaches rely on one, while a magician's timing is rehearsed and internal.
Things a magician uses.Gavel: A mallet for judges' and auctioneers' orders, though a magician has no real use for it.
Things a magician uses.Paintbrush: Brushes use animal hair or synthetic fibers, and no famous trick depends on one.
Things a magician uses.Trowel: Masons and gardeners use it, and it has nothing to do with sleight of hand despite its flat, wand-like handle.
Things a magician uses.Plunger: A rubber cup that works by suction; it appears in comedy magic only as a joke.
Things a magician uses.Hard hat: Hard hats came into use after Edward Bullard patented his Hard Boiled Hat in 1919, for builders and miners.
Things a magician uses.Microscope: The first compound microscopes appeared around 1600 in the Netherlands, long before laboratories.
Things a magician uses.Fire hose: The earliest ones were leather sewn together, invented in the 1600s by a Dutch inventor.
Things a magician uses.Spatula: From the Latin word for a flat piece of wood, it is a kitchen flipper, not a conjuring tool.
Things a magician uses.Shovel: A shovel's design has stayed close to ancient ones, and nothing about it suits stage tricks.
Things a magician uses.Briefcase: It carries papers, not rabbits, though a briefcase with a false bottom sometimes appears in comedy routines.
Things a magician uses.Pitchfork: A hay tool with long tines, closer to a devil's prop than a magician's.

Jobs at a tech company.Software engineer: Margaret Hamilton, who led Apollo's flight software team, helped popularise the term 'software engineering' in the 1960s.
Jobs at a tech company.Product manager: Decides what to build and why, and is often called the CEO of the product, though without the actual authority.
Jobs at a tech company.UX designer: Don Norman, then at Apple, is credited with coining the phrase 'user experience' in the early 1990s.
Jobs at a tech company.Data scientist: Harvard Business Review called it the 'sexiest job of the 21st century' in 2012.
Jobs at a tech company.DevOps engineer: The word blends development and operations, aiming to end the old wall between teams who write code and run it.
Jobs at a tech company.QA tester: The famous first computer 'bug' was a moth found in a Harvard Mark II relay in 1947.
Jobs at a tech company.Sysadmin: Keeps servers and networks running; System Administrator Appreciation Day falls on the last Friday of July.
Jobs at a tech company.Scrum master: Scrum is borrowed from rugby, where players pack together to restart play; software teams adopted it in the 1990s.
Jobs at a tech company.Web developer: Tim Berners-Lee wrote the first web page at CERN around 1990 and 1991.
Jobs at a tech company.Data analyst: They turn raw numbers into answers with SQL and spreadsheets, and Excel remains one of the most used tools.
Jobs at a tech company.Cloud architect: The cloud is other people's data centres, and architects design systems across them for reliability.
Jobs at a tech company.Farrier: Shoes horses; the job needs strong hands and a forge, and it has survived since the Middle Ages.
Jobs at a tech company.Chimney sweep: Cleans flues to prevent fires; in the UK, shaking hands with a sweep is considered lucky.
Jobs at a tech company.Cobbler: Repairs shoes, unlike a shoemaker who makes them new; the same word also names a fruit pudding.
Jobs at a tech company.Blacksmith: Shapes hot iron; Smith is among the most common surnames in English-speaking countries partly because of this trade.
Jobs at a tech company.Thatcher: Roofs buildings with straw or reed; a well-made reed thatch can last 40 years or more.
Jobs at a tech company.Shepherd: Looks after sheep, a job so old that Psalm 23 uses it as an image of care.
Jobs at a tech company.Lumberjack: Fells trees; the legend of Paul Bunyan, a giant logger, grew out of North American logging camps.
Jobs at a tech company.Midwife: Delivers babies, and in many countries midwives attend most births, a job thousands of years old.
Jobs at a tech company.Lifeguard: Watches swimmers for trouble, a job of sharp attention rather than code.
Jobs at a tech company.Jockey: Rides racehorses; the job rewards low body weight, not programming skill.
Jobs at a tech company.Gondolier: Guides Venetian gondolas with a single oar, a job that needs a licence, not an engineering degree.
Jobs at a tech company.Sommelier: A restaurant's wine expert; the Court of Master Sommeliers sets one of the hardest exams in food and drink.
Jobs at a tech company.Town crier: Announced news aloud before newspapers, and 'Oyez' meant listen; an early form of push notification.

Things a geologist uses.Rock hammer: Often a one-piece steel hammer with a chisel or pick end, used to break rock and reveal fresh, unweathered surfaces.
Things a geologist uses.Hand lens: A 10x magnifier on a cord; geologists hold it by the eye and bring the rock to it to see grains and crystals.
Things a geologist uses.Compass: A Brunton compass also measures strike and dip, meaning how a rock layer tilts.
Things a geologist uses.Field notebook: Notes and sketches made on the spot underpin geologic maps, so the pages are tough and weatherproof.
Things a geologist uses.Acid bottle: A drop of dilute hydrochloric acid fizzes on limestone, a quick field test for carbonate minerals.
Things a geologist uses.Streak plate: Rubbing a mineral on unglazed porcelain shows its powder colour; hematite is steel-grey but streaks red-brown.
Things a geologist uses.GPS unit: Records exact sample locations for later maps; before GPS, geologists navigated by map and compass.
Things a geologist uses.Sample bags: Each is labelled with its location, since a sample with no locality record is nearly worthless.
Things a geologist uses.Topographic map: Contour lines show elevation, and closer lines mean steeper ground, which helps geologists read landforms.
Things a geologist uses.Chisel: Chisels help extract fossils or fresh rock faces cleanly, working with a hammer.
Things a geologist uses.Hard hat: Protects from falling rock in quarries and cliffs, usually together with safety glasses.
Things a geologist uses.Stethoscope: A medical listening tool; seismologists listen to the Earth with seismometers instead.
Things a geologist uses.Telescope: Looks skyward, though planetary geologists do use telescope data to study the surfaces of other worlds.
Things a geologist uses.Whisk: A cook's tool for beating eggs; geologists working with fine sediment use sieves instead.
Things a geologist uses.Saddle: A horse's seat, which geologists may use to reach remote terrain; 'saddle' is also a type of mountain pass.
Things a geologist uses.Gavel: A judge's mallet; the geologist's hammer is the closest equivalent, but it's built to break rock.
Things a geologist uses.Easel: A painter's stand; field geologists sketch outcrops in a notebook, not on canvas.
Things a geologist uses.Loom: Weavers use it, though asbestos fibres were once woven, a case where geology met looms.
Things a geologist uses.Piping bag: A baker's icing tool; geology has pipes too, like kimberlite pipes that carry diamonds up from deep.
Things a geologist uses.Fishing rod: Used by anglers, but drillers do 'fish' for lost tools stuck in boreholes using special retrieval gear.
Things a geologist uses.Plunger: A plumber's tool for clogged drains, with no role in the field kit.
Things a geologist uses.Baton: A conductor's wand or relay runner's stick, with no use in the field.
Things a geologist uses.Lasso: A cowboy's looped rope; geologists carry rope for climbing, not for catching cattle.
Things a geologist uses.Spatula: A kitchen flipper, though a small trowel-like spatula can scoop soft sediment samples.

Marketing terms.Brand: The word comes from the Old Norse for burning, because owners literally branded cattle to mark them as theirs.
Marketing terms.Slogan: The word comes from the Gaelic for a battle cry, and today a great slogan like "Just Do It" can be worth millions.
Marketing terms.Logo: Some of the most valuable logos are strikingly simple; the Nike swoosh was bought from a design student in 1971 for just 35 dollars.
Marketing terms.Target audience: Marketers narrow it down by age, interests and habits, because a message meant for everyone often connects with no one.
Marketing terms.Campaign: The word comes from the Latin for an open field, since it began as a military term for an army's season of operations.
Marketing terms.Billboard: Roadside ads date to the 1860s, and early ones were often just paper posters pasted onto boards.
Marketing terms.Jingle: Some jingles are famously sticky, as brands know that a short tune can stay in the mind for decades.
Marketing terms.Advertisement: The oldest known ads are Egyptian papyrus notices, and one from Thebes offered a reward for a runaway slave and praised a weaver.
Marketing terms.Focus group: A small panel is asked about a product, but researchers know people can be swayed by the loudest voice in the room.
Marketing terms.Market research: Famously, New Coke tested well in blind tastings in 1985, yet customers rejected it when the real name was on the can.
Marketing terms.Rebranding: A company redesigns its identity to change perception; it can backfire, as when a rebranded logo draws a public backlash.
Marketing terms.Sauté: From the French for jumped, it describes tossing food in a hot pan; it is cooking, not advertising.
Marketing terms.Braise: Slow cooking meat in a little liquid turns tough cuts tender, but it is a kitchen term and not a marketing one.
Marketing terms.Julienne: It means cutting vegetables into thin matchsticks, a knife skill with no connection to branding.
Marketing terms.Blanch: Dipping vegetables briefly in boiling water then ice water keeps their bright color, and has nothing to do with campaigns.
Marketing terms.Flambé: Flaming alcohol in a pan burns off most of it, though some remains, and makes for good table theater in restaurants.
Marketing terms.Simmer: Simmering holds water just below boiling, around 85 to 95 degrees Celsius, a gentle heat that sells soups better than adverts.
Marketing terms.Poach: Gently cooking food in liquid; poached eggs are cooked in barely moving water, and the term is not marketing.
Marketing terms.Deglaze: Adding liquid to a hot pan lifts browned bits stuck to it, which makes the base of a flavorful sauce.
Marketing terms.Marinate: Marinades mostly flavor the surface of meat rather than soaking deeply in, which surprises many cooks.
Marketing terms.Knead: Kneading develops gluten, the stretchy protein network that gives bread its chew, and is purely a baking matter.
Marketing terms.Baste: Spooning juices over roasting meat adds flavor, although many chefs say it does little to keep the meat moist.
Marketing terms.Parboil: Parboiling partly cooks food first, and is a classic trick for crisp roast potatoes, not for ad campaigns.
Marketing terms.Caramelize: When sugar heats to around 170 degrees Celsius it turns brown and nutty, a cooking reaction rather than a marketing one.

Medical specialties.Cardiology: The heart beats around 100,000 times a day, and cardiologists treat its rhythm, valves and the arteries feeding it.
Medical specialties.Dermatology: Skin is the body's largest organ, and dermatologists also treat hair and nails.
Medical specialties.Neurology: The brain has about 86 billion neurons, and neurologists treat disorders such as epilepsy, stroke and Parkinson's disease.
Medical specialties.Oncology: Oncologists treat cancer, and the name comes from the Greek "onkos", meaning mass or lump.
Medical specialties.Pediatrics: The word comes from the Greek for child healing, and it is the specialty for children from birth to young adulthood.
Medical specialties.Radiology: X-rays were discovered by Wilhelm Roentgen in 1895, and radiologists now read X-rays, MRI and CT scans.
Medical specialties.Orthopedics: The name comes from Greek for straight child, and the original aim was to correct children's deformities.
Medical specialties.Psychiatry: Psychiatrists are medical doctors who can prescribe drugs, unlike most psychologists.
Medical specialties.Urology: The field treats the urinary tract of everyone and the male reproductive system.
Medical specialties.Gastroenterology: It covers the digestive tract, and the human gut hosts trillions of bacteria.
Medical specialties.Ophthalmology: Ophthalmologists are medical doctors for eyes, and a very common eye operation is cataract surgery.
Medical specialties.Obstetrics: It deals with pregnancy and birth, from the Latin for midwife.
Medical specialties.Astrology: A trap: it looks like a medical -ology but claims to read the stars to predict lives, and it has no scientific support.
Medical specialties.Geology: Geology is the study of rocks and the Earth, and it studies the planet, not patients.
Medical specialties.Theology: The study of religion and God, and a trap, since it ends in -ology but is not medicine.
Medical specialties.Mythology: The study of myths, such as those of the Greek and Norse, which has no clinical side.
Medical specialties.Numerology: It claims numbers hold hidden meaning, but it's a belief and not a medical field.
Medical specialties.Meteorology: It comes from the Greek for things high in the air, and it studies weather, not health.
Medical specialties.Seismology: It studies earthquakes, and seismologists use waves from them to understand Earth's interior.
Medical specialties.Graphology: The study of handwriting to judge character, which research has not supported.
Medical specialties.Criminology: It studies crime and its causes, so it belongs to social science, not medicine.
Medical specialties.Musicology: The scholarly study of music history and theory, and it doesn't need a stethoscope.
Medical specialties.Etymology: The study of word origins, and the Greek root means true sense; it doesn't deal with bugs, which is entomology.
Medical specialties.Volcanology: Volcanologists study volcanoes, and some collect samples at the very edge of lava.

Things a blacksmith makes.Horseshoes: A horseshoe is traditionally made by heating iron until orange, then hammering it into a U-shape; a farrier usually fits it.
Things a blacksmith makes.Nails: Before machines, nails were made by hand, one at a time, and a blacksmith could forge hundreds in a day.
Things a blacksmith makes.Gates: Wrought-iron gates can be both beautiful and strong, and some in old cities are centuries old.
Things a blacksmith makes.Hinges: Blacksmiths made strap hinges for castle doors and barns, and many old ones are still working today.
Things a blacksmith makes.Tongs: A blacksmith uses tongs to hold hot metal, and they often make their own to fit each shape of work.
Things a blacksmith makes.Fire pokers: These simple iron rods were forged to tend hearth fires and are among the typical beginner projects for smiths.
Things a blacksmith makes.Railings: Wrought iron railings graced Georgian and Victorian houses, and many were removed for scrap in World War II.
Things a blacksmith makes.Hooks: From coat hooks to meat hooks, they are among the simplest forged items, made by bending a hot rod.
Things a blacksmith makes.Swords: Medieval swordsmiths heated, folded and quenched steel, and Japanese katana smiths folded it to remove impurities.
Things a blacksmith makes.Chains: Each link is formed by hand from a bar, bent into a loop, and welded, a process called forge welding.
Things a blacksmith makes.Cakes: A baker's job, and the only fire involved is an oven, not a forge hot enough to melt iron.
Things a blacksmith makes.Sweaters: They are knitted from wool, and no one has ever hammered one out on an anvil.
Things a blacksmith makes.Baskets: Baskets are woven from reeds or willow by a basketmaker, and the craft is one of the oldest known.
Things a blacksmith makes.Pottery: It's shaped from clay and fired, usually between 900 and 1,300 degrees Celsius, in a kiln.
Things a blacksmith makes.Candles: A chandler dips or molds wax, and nothing gets hammered.
Things a blacksmith makes.Quilts: Quilting is done with needle and thread, and it's far from the forge.
Things a blacksmith makes.Barrels: A cooper makes them, bending wooden staves into shape with fire and steam, though iron hoops may be made by a smith.
Things a blacksmith makes.Saddles: A saddler works leather, and stirrups and buckles may come from a smith.
Things a blacksmith makes.Wigs: A wigmaker uses hair, with no forge involved.
Things a blacksmith makes.Shoes: A cobbler or shoemaker sews them from leather, while the smith made the horse's.
Things a blacksmith makes.Hats: A milliner or hatter makes them from felt, straw or fabric.
Things a blacksmith makes.Rope: A ropemaker twists fibers into strands, and long rope walks were once needed for the navy.
Things a blacksmith makes.Soap: It is made from fat and alkali, with no metal forging involved.
Things a blacksmith makes.Leather belts: A leatherworker makes the belt, though the buckle might well be forged by a smith.

Wired computer ports and connectors.USB-C: USB-C is reversible, so there's no wrong way to plug it in. The EU made it the common charging port for phones sold there from 2024.
Wired computer ports and connectors.HDMI: HDMI carries video and sound through one cable. It was introduced in 2003, and it succeeded older analog connections like component video.
Wired computer ports and connectors.Ethernet: Ethernet was invented at Xerox PARC in 1973 by Robert Metcalfe. Wired connections still beat Wi-Fi for steady speed and low delay.
Wired computer ports and connectors.VGA: VGA, introduced by IBM in 1987, was an analog video port with 15 pins. Its blue connector remained on monitors well into the 2010s.
Wired computer ports and connectors.DisplayPort: DisplayPort came from the VESA group in 2006 to replace VGA and DVI. It can send video to several monitors through one connection.
Wired computer ports and connectors.Lightning: Apple's Lightning connector appeared in 2012 with the iPhone 5, replacing the wider 30-pin dock. It's reversible, and Apple later moved iPhones to USB-C.
Wired computer ports and connectors.Thunderbolt: Thunderbolt was developed by Intel with Apple, which first used it in 2011. It carries data, video and power through a single cable.
Wired computer ports and connectors.Headphone jack: The 3.5 mm jack's ancestors were in old telephone switchboards. Apple dropped it from the iPhone in 2016, to considerable debate.
Wired computer ports and connectors.Micro-USB: Micro-USB ruled Android charging in the 2010s. It could be inserted only one way, and it was gradually replaced by USB-C.
Wired computer ports and connectors.DVI: DVI arrived in 1999 to bring digital video to monitors. It was a bridge between the old analog VGA world and HDMI.
Wired computer ports and connectors.FireWire: FireWire was Apple's name for IEEE 1394, a fast data port of the 1990s. It was widely used for digital camcorders, then displaced by USB.
Wired computer ports and connectors.Bluetooth: Bluetooth is wireless, so no cable is involved. It's named after a Viking-era Danish king, Harald Bluetooth, who united tribes.
Wired computer ports and connectors.Wi-Fi: Wi-Fi is a wireless networking standard, so it needs no physical connector. The name has no deeper meaning and doesn't stand for "wireless fidelity."
Wired computer ports and connectors.NFC: Near-field communication works only within a few centimeters. It powers tap-to-pay, and it uses radio rather than a cable.
Wired computer ports and connectors.5G: 5G is the fifth generation of mobile networks, carried by radio waves. There's no port involved, and your phone connects to towers.
Wired computer ports and connectors.Infrared: Infrared remotes send invisible light pulses to TVs. Infrared is wireless, though it needs a clear line of sight.
Wired computer ports and connectors.AirDrop: AirDrop is Apple's wireless file sharing, using Bluetooth and Wi-Fi to find nearby devices. No wire is needed.
Wired computer ports and connectors.Zigbee: Zigbee is a low-power wireless protocol for smart-home gadgets. The name refers to the zigzag dance of bees.
Wired computer ports and connectors.LTE: LTE is a 4G mobile data standard, and stands for Long-Term Evolution. It travels by radio, not through a cable.
Wired computer ports and connectors.Satellite: Satellite internet bounces signals through space, and the dish connects to your home by cable. The link itself is wireless.
Wired computer ports and connectors.GPS: GPS receivers pick up signals from satellites about 20,000 km up. It's a wireless positioning system, not a port.
Wired computer ports and connectors.AirPlay: AirPlay is Apple's wireless streaming system for audio and video. As the name suggests, it works through the air.
Wired computer ports and connectors.Radio: Radio carries signals through the air using electromagnetic waves. It's the foundation of many wireless technologies, not a physical port.
Wired computer ports and connectors.Chromecast: Chromecast is a Google dongle that plugs into a TV's HDMI port, but it receives content wirelessly. Its streaming itself isn't wired.

Adobe products.Photoshop: First released in 1990, Photoshop became so common that its name turned into a verb for editing images.
Adobe products.Illustrator: Illustrator makes vector graphics, built from math rather than pixels, so logos can scale from a business card to a billboard.
Adobe products.Premiere Pro: A pro video editor used on feature films and TV shows, and a direct competitor to Apple's Final Cut Pro.
Adobe products.After Effects: The go-to tool for motion graphics, used to make animated titles and visual effects in films and online videos.
Adobe products.InDesign: InDesign lays out magazines and books, and it replaced Adobe's older PageMaker in 1999 as the industry standard.
Adobe products.Acrobat: Acrobat reads and edits PDFs, the format Adobe invented in the early 1990s so documents would look identical anywhere.
Adobe products.Lightroom: Lightroom organizes and edits photos non-destructively, so the original file stays untouched.
Adobe products.Dreamweaver: Dreamweaver was a popular web design tool of the 1990s and 2000s, from Macromedia, which Adobe bought in 2005.
Adobe products.Flash: Flash powered web animations and games for years before Adobe officially ended support at the end of 2020.
Adobe products.Audition: Adobe's audio editor descended from Cool Edit Pro, which Adobe acquired in 2003 from Syntrillium Software.
Adobe products.Firefly: Firefly is Adobe's generative AI family, trained on licensed images.
Adobe products.Final Cut Pro: Final Cut Pro is Apple's video editor, a rival of Adobe's Premiere.
Adobe products.GarageBand: GarageBand is Apple's free music creation app.
Adobe products.iMovie: Apple's free video editor comes on Macs and iPhones, so it's a rival to Adobe's Premiere rather than one of its products.
Adobe products.Canva: Canva is an Australian online design tool aimed at non-designers, and it has become a major Adobe rival.
Adobe products.GIMP: GIMP is a free open-source image editor and a rival to Photoshop.
Adobe products.Blender: Blender is a free 3D tool, not made by Adobe.
Adobe products.Figma: Figma is a design tool Adobe tried to buy for 20 billion dollars in 2022 but abandoned over regulators.
Adobe products.Paint: Paint is the basic drawing app built into Windows since 1985, and Microsoft's, not Adobe's.
Adobe products.Procreate: Procreate is a popular iPad drawing app from an Australian company, and it competes with Adobe's tools.
Adobe products.AutoCAD: AutoCAD is design software from Autodesk.
Adobe products.Logic Pro: Logic Pro is Apple's professional music software.
Adobe products.Sketch: Sketch is a Mac design tool for interfaces, made by a Dutch company, which was an early rival to Adobe XD.

Computing pioneers.Alan Turing: He helped crack Germany's Enigma code in World War II and in 1936 described the abstract Turing machine, the theory behind all computers.
Computing pioneers.Ada Lovelace: Lord Byron's daughter wrote what is often called the first computer algorithm in 1843, for Babbage's Analytical Engine.
Computing pioneers.Charles Babbage: He designed mechanical computers in the 1800s; a Difference Engine built from his plans in 1991 worked perfectly.
Computing pioneers.Grace Hopper: She created one of the first compilers and popularized the term 'bug' after a moth was found in a Harvard computer in 1947.
Computing pioneers.Tim Berners-Lee: He proposed the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN and never patented it, so anyone could use it.
Computing pioneers.John von Neumann: The stored-program design behind nearly every computer is named after this Hungarian-American mathematician.
Computing pioneers.Dennis Ritchie: He created the C language and co-created Unix, and died in 2011, just days after Steve Jobs.
Computing pioneers.Linus Torvalds: He began Linux in 1991 as a hobby project and later created Git, the tool most programmers use for version control.
Computing pioneers.Vint Cerf: He co-designed TCP/IP with Bob Kahn in the 1970s, the protocols on which the internet runs, and is called one of its fathers.
Computing pioneers.Margaret Hamilton: She led the software team for the Apollo missions and coined 'software engineering'; a stack of its printouts matched her height.
Computing pioneers.Claude Shannon: The father of information theory; he popularized the 'bit' and in his spare time rode a unicycle through the halls of Bell Labs.
Computing pioneers.Isaac Newton: Newton invented calculus and gravity theory, but he predates computers by centuries.
Computing pioneers.Albert Einstein: His physics changed the world, though he never built computers, even though the Institute for Advanced Study where he worked built an early one.
Computing pioneers.Marie Curie: A two-time Nobel winner for physics and chemistry, who studied radioactivity rather than computing.
Computing pioneers.Charles Darwin: His theory of evolution later inspired genetic algorithms, but he lived a century before computers.
Computing pioneers.Galileo: An astronomy and physics pioneer who improved the telescope; he lived four centuries before modern computers.
Computing pioneers.Leonardo da Vinci: A brilliant inventor on paper, but his notebooks held no computing machines that were ever built.
Computing pioneers.Stephen Hawking: The physicist used a speech synthesizer to communicate, making him a computer user rather than a pioneer.
Computing pioneers.Carl Sagan: The astronomer and science popularizer, famous for Cosmos, but not a computing figure.
Computing pioneers.Jane Goodall: Famous for her decades of chimpanzee research in Tanzania, not computing.
Computing pioneers.Louis Pasteur: His work on vaccines and pasteurization saved countless lives but had nothing to do with computing.
Computing pioneers.Sigmund Freud: The founder of psychoanalysis, whose work was in the mind rather than machines.
Computing pioneers.Gregor Mendel: The monk whose pea plant experiments founded genetics, with no link to computing.
Computing pioneers.Neil Armstrong: He walked on the Moon in 1969, using software that Margaret Hamilton's team wrote.

Physical media formats.VHS: JVC's tape format beat Betamax in the 1980s home video war, partly because its tapes recorded for longer.
