Physical media formats.Betamax: Sony's format was often judged sharper but lost the format war; Sony only stopped selling new Betamax tapes in 2016.
Physical media formats.Cassette: Philips introduced the compact cassette in 1963, and it made homemade mixtapes and the portable Walkman possible.
Physical media formats.CD: Co-developed by Philips and Sony, the first CDs went on sale in 1982. A popular story says its size was set to fit Beethoven's Ninth.
Physical media formats.DVD: A single-layer DVD holds about 4.7 GB, roughly seven times a CD, which was enough for a feature film.
Physical media formats.Blu-ray: Named for the blue-violet laser that reads it, whose short wavelength packs far more data than a DVD. It beat HD DVD in 2008.
Physical media formats.LaserDisc: Pioneer's 12-inch optical discs stored analog video, and Criterion's King Kong release is often credited with the first commentary track.
Physical media formats.MiniDisc: Sony's 1992 pocket-sized recordable disc, popular in Japan, never really caught on elsewhere.
Physical media formats.8-track: Car stereos loved these looping tape cartridges in the 1960s and 70s, though switching programs could cut a song in half.
Physical media formats.Vinyl record: Vinyl sales have been climbing for years, and in some years records have outsold CDs in the US.
Physical media formats.Floppy disk: The 3.5-inch version held just 1.44 MB, yet its picture lives on as the universal save icon.
Physical media formats.UMD: Sony's tiny optical disc for the PSP held about 1.8 GB and flopped as a movie format.
Physical media formats.MP3: A trap: it's a file format, not a physical object. It compresses audio and took off in the late 1990s.
Physical media formats.Spotify: A streaming service from Sweden launched in 2008, where you rent access instead of owning any physical copy.
Physical media formats.Netflix: A trap with a past: it started by mailing DVDs in 1998, but today it streams, so it's a service, not a format.
Physical media formats.Streaming: Content delivered over the internet as you watch, so there's nothing to hold, which is why it has displaced much physical media.
Physical media formats.Podcast: The word blends iPod and broadcast. Episodes are digital audio files delivered through an RSS feed, no disc needed.
Physical media formats.iCloud: Apple's online storage service from 2011 keeps your files on remote servers, so there's nothing physical to hold.
Physical media formats.JPEG: Named for the Joint Photographic Experts Group that created it, it's an image compression format, not a medium.
Physical media formats.Wi-Fi: A wireless networking standard, not a storage medium. The name was invented by a branding firm and doesn't really stand for anything.
Physical media formats.Download: Saving a file from the internet to your device is an action, and it's how digital downloads made the disc unnecessary.
Physical media formats.iTunes: Apple's software and store launched in 2001. It sold digital songs, so there was no physical copy.
Physical media formats.Torrent: Peer-to-peer sharing where pieces of a file arrive from many users at once. It's a transfer method, not a format.
Physical media formats.Bluetooth: A wireless link named after Harald Bluetooth, a Danish king who united tribes, which makes it a connection, not a medium.

Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Walkman: Sony's 1979 cassette player sold over 200 million units; it was reportedly nearly named Soundabout or Stowaway in some markets.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.VCR: The 1980s VHS versus Betamax format war ended with VHS winning, largely because its tapes could record longer.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Boombox: Also called a ghetto blaster, it carried hip-hop out of living rooms and onto city streets, and its size made it a status symbol.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Rotary phone: A rotary dial sends pulses, one per number, so dialing a 9 or 0 took far longer than dialing a 1.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Atari 2600: Launched in 1977, it was still selling in the 1980s, and its famously buried E.T. cartridges reportedly ended up in a New Mexico landfill.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Cassette player: Cassettes let people make mixtapes, and a 1980s music industry campaign claimed that home taping was killing music.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Answering machine: Early home models recorded callers on tiny tapes, and the 1980s boom made screening your calls a new habit.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Camcorder: Sony's 1985 Handycam made home video mainstream, and the first TV clips of everyday family life soon followed.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Commodore 64: Released in 1982, it is often cited as the best-selling single computer model ever, at roughly 12 to 17 million units.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Microwave: Percy Spencer reportedly noticed a candy bar melting in his pocket near a radar tube, which led to the microwave oven.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Pocket calculator: Early 1970s models cost hundreds of dollars, but by the 1980s some solar-powered ones were as thin as a credit card.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Digital watch: The 1970s LED watch was a luxury, but by the 1980s cheap LCD watches like Casio's were everywhere, often with built-in calculators.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.iPhone: It arrived in 2007, about 27 years after the decade ended, so the closest 1980s equivalent was a brick-sized car phone.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Smart speaker: The first mainstream one, Amazon's Echo, came out in 2014, so nothing in the 1980s could answer voice questions.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Roomba: iRobot launched it in 2002, more than a decade after the 1980s, when robot vacuums existed only in science fiction.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.DVD player: DVDs appeared in 1996 and 1997, so 1980s movie fans were stuck with tape or the short-lived LaserDisc.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Wi-Fi router: Wi-Fi was standardized in 1997, so in the 1980s a home network meant a phone line and a slow modem at best.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Blu-ray player: Blu-ray debuted in 2006, and its name comes from the blue-violet laser that reads its dense discs.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Fitbit: The first Fitbit tracker appeared in 2009, when step counting in the 1980s meant a mechanical pedometer.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.AirPods: Apple released them in 2016, so 1980s listeners were tangled in the cords of foam-covered Walkman headphones.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Kindle: Amazon's e-reader dates from 2007, though the 1980s did have electronic dictionaries with tiny screens.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.Flash drive: USB sticks appeared around 2000, so 1980s files traveled on floppy disks holding well under two megabytes.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.MP3 player: The MP3 format was finished in the 1990s and portable players came in 1998, long after the 1980s Walkman.
Gadgets that existed in the 1980s.iPod: It was launched in 2001 with 1,000 songs in your pocket, which the 1980s Walkman could never manage.

Games made by Blizzard.World of Warcraft: Launched in 2004, it peaked at over 12 million subscribers around 2010 and still hosts some of gaming's longest-running guilds.
Games made by Blizzard.StarCraft: In South Korea this 1998 strategy game became a national esport, with pro gamers, sponsors and TV channels devoted to matches.
Games made by Blizzard.Diablo: The 1996 original popularized the loot-hunting action RPG, and its randomly generated dungeons mean no two descents are alike.
Games made by Blizzard.Overwatch: Blizzard built it from the wreckage of Titan, an ambitious MMO cancelled in 2014 after years of development.
Games made by Blizzard.Hearthstone: Started by a small team as a side project, this 2014 card game pulled tens of millions into duels set in a Warcraft tavern.
Games made by Blizzard.Warcraft III: Its map editor birthed Defense of the Ancients, the fan mod that led to the whole MOBA genre, including Dota 2 and League of Legends.
Games made by Blizzard.Heroes of the Storm: A crossover MOBA from 2015 where Warcraft, Diablo and StarCraft heroes brawl on one map, with no shop to buy items.
Games made by Blizzard.The Lost Vikings: Blizzard's 1992 puzzle-platformer, made when it was still Silicon & Synapse, starred three Vikings who later became playable heroes in Heroes of the Storm.
Games made by Blizzard.Warcraft Rumble: Released in 2023, this was the first Warcraft game built for phones, a tower-defense-flavored battler using tiny miniatures.
Games made by Blizzard.Fortnite: Epic Games made it. It debuted in 2017 as a co-op zombie-defense game before its battle royale mode took over the world.
Games made by Blizzard.League of Legends: Riot Games' 2009 hit grew from the Warcraft III mod scene, but the company has no connection to Blizzard.
Games made by Blizzard.Dota 2: Valve's 2013 sequel to a Warcraft III mod. Blizzard's editor made the original possible, but Blizzard didn't make this.
Games made by Blizzard.Halo: Bungie built it, not Blizzard. It was first shown in 1999 as a Mac game, then Microsoft bought Bungie in 2000 and made it an Xbox launch title.
Games made by Blizzard.Destiny: Bungie's 2014 shared-world shooter was published by Activision, which later merged with Blizzard, but Blizzard didn't make it.
Games made by Blizzard.Call of Duty: Made by Activision's studios, not Blizzard, though the two shared a parent and Call of Duty has been sold on Battle.net since 2016.
Games made by Blizzard.Apex Legends: Respawn Entertainment released this in 2019 with no advance announcement and reportedly reached 25 million players in a week.
Games made by Blizzard.Valorant: Riot Games' 2020 tactical shooter. Blizzard's own hero shooter is Overwatch, so this one is a rival, not a sibling.
Games made by Blizzard.Half-Life: Valve's 1998 shooter, famous for storytelling without cutscenes. Its fan mod Counter-Strike later became even bigger.
Games made by Blizzard.Minecraft: Mojang's game, not Blizzard's. Microsoft bought the studio for about 2.5 billion dollars in 2014, and it is the best-selling game ever.
Games made by Blizzard.Guild Wars: ArenaNet's 2005 MMO had no monthly fee, a deliberate contrast to World of Warcraft's subscription model.
Games made by Blizzard.EverQuest: Sony's 1999 MMO, nicknamed EverCrack for its addictive pull, was the genre leader until World of Warcraft overtook it.
Games made by Blizzard.RuneScape: Britain's Jagex built it as a browser game in 2001, and it remains one of the most played MMOs, with no Blizzard link.
Games made by Blizzard.Team Fortress 2: Valve's 2007 class-based shooter is often cited as a forerunner of Overwatch's hero style, but it isn't a Blizzard game.
Games made by Blizzard.Crash Bandicoot: The marsupial mascot debuted on PlayStation in 1996 from Naughty Dog. Activision later owned the brand, but Blizzard never made it.

Dogs in literature.Toto: Toto is Dorothy's Cairn terrier in The Wizard of Oz, and in the 1939 film, the dog was paid more than many actors.
Dogs in literature.Buck: Buck is the St. Bernard mix in Jack London's The Call of the Wild who returns to the wild in the Yukon gold rush.
Dogs in literature.Lassie: Lassie is the collie from Eric Knight's 1940 story, and the dog in the TV and film versions was played by male dogs.
Dogs in literature.Old Yeller: Old Yeller is the stray yellow dog in Fred Gipson's 1956 Texas novel, which broke a generation's hearts.
Dogs in literature.Clifford: Clifford is the giant red dog of Norman Bridwell's picture books, who is as tall as a house.
Dogs in literature.Nana: Nana is the Darling children's Newfoundland nursemaid in Peter Pan, who bathes them and tucks them in.
Dogs in literature.Bull's-eye: Bull's-eye is Bill Sikes's terrier in Oliver Twist, whose loyal and bloody end follows his master's.
Dogs in literature.Fang: Fang is Hagrid's cowardly boarhound, a big dog who is afraid of almost everything.
Dogs in literature.Fluffy: Fluffy is the three-headed dog that guards the Philosopher's Stone, and music lulls him asleep.
Dogs in literature.Argos: Argos is Odysseus's old hound, who recognizes his master after twenty years, then dies, in the Odyssey.
Dogs in literature.Shiloh: Shiloh is a beagle in Phyllis Reynolds Naylor's novel, which won the Newbery Medal in 1992.
Dogs in literature.Snowy: Snowy is Tintin's fox terrier, called Milou in French, who often comments on events with his thoughts.
Dogs in literature.Garfield: Garfield is a cartoon cat created by Jim Davis in 1978, who hates Mondays and loves lasagna.
Dogs in literature.Crookshanks: Crookshanks is Hermione's cat, part Kneazle, who is smart enough to spot that Scabbers isn't really a rat.
Dogs in literature.Mrs Norris: Mrs Norris is Filch's dusty gray cat, who patrols for rule-breaking students.
Dogs in literature.Hedwig: Hedwig is Harry's snowy owl, a gift from Hagrid for his birthday, and she delivers his post.
Dogs in literature.Cheshire Cat: The Cheshire Cat is a grinning cat in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland who can vanish until only its smile is left.
Dogs in literature.Aslan: Aslan is the lion who creates Narnia, and C. S. Lewis made him a Christ-like figure.
Dogs in literature.Bagheera: Bagheera is the black panther who teaches Mowgli in The Jungle Book, not a dog.
Dogs in literature.Black Beauty: Black Beauty is a horse who tells his story in Anna Sewell's 1877 novel, so not a dog.
Dogs in literature.Shadowfax: Shadowfax is Gandalf's horse, the lord of the Mearas, the fastest in Rohan.
Dogs in literature.Templeton: Templeton is the greedy rat in Charlotte's Web, who helps only when there's food.
Dogs in literature.Tom Kitten: Tom Kitten is a Beatrix Potter cat who loses his clothes and is rolled in pastry by rats.
Dogs in literature.Puss in Boots: Puss in Boots is Perrault's clever cat who wins a fortune for his master, not a dog.

Characters in Twelfth Night.Viola: Shipwrecked, she disguises herself as the page Cesario. In Shakespeare's day a boy actor played her pretending to be a boy.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Sebastian: Viola's twin brother. Olivia mistaking him for Cesario creates the confusion that resolves into a happy ending.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Orsino: The duke opens the play with "If music be the food of love, play on", then spends it pining for Olivia.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Olivia: A countess in mourning who falls for the disguised Viola, and then marries Sebastian by mistake.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Malvolio: The pompous steward tricked by a forged letter into wearing yellow stockings, and he exits swearing, "I'll be revenged on the whole pack of you!"
Characters in Twelfth Night.Sir Toby Belch: Olivia's hard-drinking uncle, whose surname hints at his habits. He leads the prank on Malvolio and ends up marrying Maria.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Sir Andrew Aguecheek: The foolish knight Toby is milking for money, bankrolling dinners while pretending to help him woo Olivia.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Maria: Olivia's gentlewoman, who forges the letter that undoes Malvolio, and who marries Toby by the end.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Feste: Olivia's jester sings the closing song "The rain it raineth every day" and is arguably the wisest person in the play.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Antonio: A sea captain who saves Sebastian and is arrested. He shares a name with the merchant of Venice but they are unrelated.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Fabian: A servant in Olivia's household who joins the plot against Malvolio, and later helps untangle the forged-letter trick at the end.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Rosalind: The heroine of As You Like It also disguises herself as a boy, but she belongs to another comedy. Hers is Shakespeare's longest female role.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Celia: Rosalind's cousin and companion in As You Like It, who follows her into the Forest of Arden.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Orlando: The lovesick hero of As You Like It, who nails bad poems to trees for Rosalind. He belongs to the Forest of Arden, not Illyria.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Touchstone: The court jester of As You Like It, who follows Rosalind into the forest. Twelfth Night's fool is Feste, not him.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Jaques: The melancholy lord who delivers the "All the world's a stage" speech, in As You Like It. Wrong play for this list.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Beatrice: She trades barbs with Benedick in Much Ado About Nothing, a model for the romantic comedy banter ever since.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Benedick: Much Ado's sharp-tongued bachelor. His name has even become a word, "benedict", for a newly married man.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Hero: Beatrice's cousin in Much Ado About Nothing, falsely accused of being unfaithful on her wedding day, a plot far from Illyria.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Claudio: Much Ado's young soldier, who publicly shames Hero at the altar on false evidence. He appears in a different comedy.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Portia: The Merchant of Venice's heiress, who disguises herself as a lawyer. She's also the name of Brutus's wife in Julius Caesar.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Bassanio: The Merchant of Venice's suitor, who wins Portia by correctly choosing the lead casket. He has no ties to Illyria.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Puck: Oberon's sprite, also called Robin Goodfellow, in A Midsummer Night's Dream. He mistakenly makes the wrong people fall in love.
Characters in Twelfth Night.Bottom: The weaver in A Midsummer Night's Dream, given a donkey's head by Puck. He has nothing to do with Illyria.

Forms of live theater.Opera: Early Florentine opera around 1600 was an attempt to revive Greek tragedy, which its inventors believed had been sung throughout.
Forms of live theater.Ballet: Ballet's French terms trace to Louis XIV's court; the Sun King danced in it himself and founded the first dance academy in 1661.
Forms of live theater.Musical: Show Boat (1927) is often called the first fully integrated musical, where songs drive the story instead of pausing it.
Forms of live theater.Pantomime: British panto tradition includes a man playing the dame and kids yelling "He's behind you!" to warn the unaware hero.
Forms of live theater.Mime: Marcel Marceau, the most famous modern mime, was a French Resistance member who helped smuggle Jewish children to safety in WWII.
Forms of live theater.Farce: The word comes from Latin farcire, "to stuff", because comic scenes were once stuffed into serious religious plays.
Forms of live theater.Melodrama: Literally "song drama": 19th-century stage melodramas had live music underscoring every thrilling or tearful moment.
Forms of live theater.Vaudeville: From the 1880s to the 1930s, vaudeville strung together unrelated acts, such as jugglers, singers and comics, on one bill.
Forms of live theater.Improv: Improv grew from Viola Spolin's theater games and Chicago's Second City, where performers live by the "yes, and" rule.
Forms of live theater.Kabuki: Said to be founded in early 1600s Japan by a female dancer, Izumo no Okuni, kabuki is now performed by men in bold makeup.
Forms of live theater.Noh: This slow 14th-century Japanese form is performed on a nearly bare stage with a painted pine tree on the back wall.
Forms of live theater.Cabaret: Cabaret began in Paris in 1881 at Le Chat Noir, where people sat at tables drinking while watching satirical songs and sketches.
Forms of live theater.Puppetry: In Japanese bunraku, each big puppet is worked by three handlers in plain view of the audience, in near-perfect sync.
Forms of live theater.Sitcom: A sitcom is made for screens, though I Love Lucy pioneered filming one with several cameras before a live studio audience.
Forms of live theater.Podcast: The word blends "iPod" and "broadcast" and dates to 2004, so it's a recorded audio format rather than a stage form.
Forms of live theater.Documentary: Scottish filmmaker John Grierson coined "documentary" in 1926 while reviewing Flaherty's Moana, so it's a film genre.
Forms of live theater.Sonnet: Shakespeare wrote 154 sonnets, but a sonnet is a 14-line poem; one even appears as the prologue of Romeo and Juliet.
Forms of live theater.Novella: A novella runs roughly 20,000 to 40,000 words, so it's something you read rather than watch performed on a stage.
Forms of live theater.Mural: Greek for a "gathering of flowers", an anthology collects writings between covers rather than putting actors on stage.
Forms of live theater.Fresco: A mural is painted straight onto a wall; Diego Rivera's enormous ones made the form famous, but nothing is performed.
Forms of live theater.Sculpture: Fresco means "fresh": pigment goes on wet plaster, as in Michelangelo's Sistine ceiling. It's painting, not performance.
Forms of live theater.Anthology: Greek and Roman statues were originally painted in bright colors; sculpture is a fixed art object, not live performance.
Forms of live theater.Reality TV: Reality TV is a television format; the US edition of Survivor in 2000 helped make it a global mainstream hit.
Forms of live theater.Vlog: A vlog is a video blog made for screens; Adam Kontras is often credited with posting the first in 2000.

Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Victor Frankenstein: Frankenstein is the scientist's name, not the monster's; Victor builds his creature from his university studies in natural philosophy.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).The Creature: Nameless in the novel, he teaches himself to speak by spying on a family and learns to read from Paradise Lost.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Elizabeth Lavenza: Victor's adopted cousin and bride is murdered on their wedding night by the Creature.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Henry Clerval: Victor's loyal friend from Geneva, whose murder by the Creature devastates him.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Robert Walton: An Arctic explorer whose letters to his sister frame the whole story as Victor tells it aboard his ship.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Justine Moritz: The Frankenstein family's servant is wrongly executed for the murder of William.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).William Frankenstein: Victor's youngest brother is the Creature's first victim, strangled in the woods near Geneva.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).De Lacey: The kind blind old man in the cottage is the one person who listens to the Creature without fear.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Safie: She is an Arab woman whose language lessons let the Creature learn French by listening in.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Igor: Igor is not in the novel; he appears in later films, where the hunchbacked assistant started as Fritz in 1931.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Dracula: Bram Stoker's Dracula was published in 1897; the vampire is not from Mary Shelley's book.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Van Helsing: Van Helsing hunts Dracula in Stoker's novel, not in Frankenstein.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Renfield: Renfield is Dracula's insect-eating madman, from Stoker's novel.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Dr. Jekyll: Stevenson's Jekyll and Hyde appeared in 1886, a separate tale of a scientist and his alter ego.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Mr. Hyde: Hyde is Jekyll's brutish alter ego, from Stevenson's 1886 novella.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Dorian Gray: Wilde's 1890 portrait-obsessed Dorian Gray is not related to Frankenstein, though both are Gothic.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Captain Nemo: Jules Verne's submarine captain is French science fiction, from 1870.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Dr. Moreau: H. G. Wells's mad scientist makes human-animals on an island, a different novel.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Quasimodo: Victor Hugo's bell-ringer belongs to Notre-Dame de Paris.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Mina Harker: Mina is Jonathan Harker's wife and Dracula's target, in Stoker's novel.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).The Invisible Man: Wells's The Invisible Man appeared in 1897, a different scientist and a different monster.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Doctor Faustus: Marlowe's Doctor Faustus sells his soul to the devil; Frankenstein's subtitle is The Modern Prometheus.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Lord Byron: In 1816 Lord Byron hosted the ghost-story contest at Villa Diodati that inspired the novel, but he is not in it.
Characters in Frankenstein (the novel).Mary Shelley: Mary Shelley began writing it at 18 during a rainy 1816 holiday, and published it anonymously in 1818.

Very loud things.Jet engine: Standing near a jet at takeoff exposes you to about 140 decibels, loud enough to cause pain, which is why ground crews wear ear protection.
Very loud things.Fireworks: A large aerial shell can produce well over 150 decibels at its source, which is why shows are watched from a safe distance.
Very loud things.Thunder: Thunder is the shock wave from lightning heating air suddenly, and you can estimate the distance by counting about three seconds per kilometer.
Very loud things.Rock concert: Rock concerts often exceed 100 decibels, and hearing damage can set in within minutes without earplugs.
Very loud things.Jackhammer: A jackhammer produces roughly 100 to 110 decibels, a noise level that damages hearing after only a few minutes.
Very loud things.Police siren: Sirens sweep through pitches because a changing sound is harder for the brain to ignore, and they hit about 120 decibels.
Very loud things.Chainsaw: A chainsaw produces around 110 decibels, so professional loggers rely on hearing protection every shift.
Very loud things.Air horn: A handheld air horn is around 120 decibels, and a train's horn can be even louder, up to about 150 at its source.
Very loud things.Rocket launch: Rocket engines are so loud that NASA sprays water onto the launchpad to absorb sound waves, which can otherwise damage the spacecraft.
Very loud things.Vuvuzela: The plastic horn, loud at about 120 decibels, shot to fame at the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, where broadcasters complained about the drone.
Very loud things.Smoke alarm: A smoke alarm must sound at about 85 decibels at ten feet, and its high pitch is picked because it wakes sleepers.
Very loud things.Leaf blower: A gas leaf blower can reach about 100 decibels, and some cities have banned them for noise.
Very loud things.Whisper: A whisper is about 30 decibels, among the quietest sounds in everyday life, and it is the very opposite of a shout.
Very loud things.Butterfly: Butterfly wings beat silently to human ears, and a flutter does not register on a typical sound meter.
Very loud things.Falling feather: A feather drifting to the floor is essentially silent, partly because its low weight and large drag make it fall at slow speed.
Very loud things.Snowfall: Snow absorbs sound with its many air pockets, which is why a fresh snowfall makes the world feel strangely hushed.
Very loud things.Library: Library quiet is about 40 decibels, roughly the same as a quiet refrigerator hum, though it feels silent.
Very loud things.Cat purring: A purr is about 25 to 30 hertz, a low rumble that is quiet in volume but is thought to help bones and tissue heal.
Very loud things.Wristwatch tick: A mechanical watch ticks softly at about 4 to 8 beats each second, quiet enough to hear only up close.
Very loud things.Mouse: Mice make squeaks, many of them in ultrasound beyond human hearing, so they sound quieter than they really are.
Very loud things.Turning a page: Page rustling is only about 20 to 30 decibels, a sound so soft that it disappears with any background noise.
Very loud things.Ant: Ants communicate with chemicals and touch, and their footsteps are too soft for human ears to catch.
Very loud things.Sunrise: Sunrise is silent, since sound doesn't travel through the vacuum of space, so there is no way to hear the Sun at all.
Very loud things.Goldfish: Goldfish do make small sounds, yet nothing a person would hear, and they can hear well using their inner ear.

Things taller than a giraffe.Redwood tree: Coast redwoods are the tallest living things; one called Hyperion is about 116 meters, around 20 giraffes stacked up.
Things taller than a giraffe.Eiffel Tower: At about 330 meters, the Eiffel Tower was the world's tallest structure for 41 years, until 1930.
Things taller than a giraffe.Brachiosaurus: Brachiosaurus held its head around 12 meters off the ground, more than twice a giraffe's height.
Things taller than a giraffe.Telephone pole: A typical utility pole stands about 10 meters above ground, roughly twice a giraffe.
Things taller than a giraffe.Statue of Liberty: The Statue of Liberty reaches about 93 meters from ground to torch, taller than 15 giraffes.
Things taller than a giraffe.London Eye: The London Eye stands 135 meters tall and was the world's tallest Ferris wheel when it opened in 2000.
Things taller than a giraffe.Lighthouse: Many lighthouses top 30 meters, and the tallest in the world stands over 100 meters, in Saudi Arabia.
Things taller than a giraffe.Christ the Redeemer: Rio's Christ the Redeemer is about 30 meters tall, plus an 8-meter pedestal, with a 28-meter arm span.
Things taller than a giraffe.Big Ben: Big Ben is the bell's name; the tower is Elizabeth Tower, standing about 96 meters tall.
Things taller than a giraffe.Space Needle: The Space Needle is 605 feet, about 184 meters, taller than a tower of 30 giraffes.
Things taller than a giraffe.Double-decker bus: A London double-decker bus is about 4.4 meters tall, just shy of a very tall giraffe, which can reach 5.5 meters.
Things taller than a giraffe.Elephant: African elephants stand roughly 3 to 4 meters at the shoulder, so a giraffe still towers over them.
Things taller than a giraffe.Basketball hoop: A basketball rim is 3.05 meters, which is lower than a giraffe's head.
Things taller than a giraffe.Grizzly bear: A grizzly standing on its hind legs reaches about 2.5 meters, shorter than a giraffe.
Things taller than a giraffe.Moai statue: The average moai is about 4 meters tall, close to a giraffe, though the biggest unfinished one is far taller.
Things taller than a giraffe.Front door: A standard door is about 2 meters, less than half a giraffe's height.
Things taller than a giraffe.Stop sign: A stop sign usually tops out at 2 to 2.5 meters, far below a giraffe.
Things taller than a giraffe.Ostrich: An ostrich, the tallest bird, reaches up to about 2.7 meters, about half a giraffe.
Things taller than a giraffe.Polar bear: A standing polar bear reaches about 3 meters, still shorter than a giraffe.
Things taller than a giraffe.Camel: Camels stand about 2 meters at the hump, while their heads sit higher but still below a giraffe's.
Things taller than a giraffe.School bus: A US school bus stands roughly 3.2 meters tall, much shorter than a giraffe.
Things taller than a giraffe.Shaquille O'Neal: Shaquille O'Neal is about 2.16 meters tall, which makes even him less than half a giraffe.
Things taller than a giraffe.Refrigerator: A typical refrigerator is about 1.8 meters, and a giraffe would look over it easily.
Things taller than a giraffe.Moose: Moose stand about 2 meters at the shoulder, big for deer but less than half a giraffe.

Volkswagen models.Beetle: More than 21 million original Beetles were built, and it overtook the Model T as the best-selling single design of its era.
Volkswagen models.Golf: The Golf took over from the Beetle in 1974, and its name comes from the Gulf Stream, not the sport.
Volkswagen models.Polo: The Polo began in 1975 as a smaller sibling to the Golf, and was based on an Audi model.
Volkswagen models.Passat: Passat is German for 'trade wind', part of Volkswagen's habit of naming cars after winds and currents.
Volkswagen models.Jetta: The Jetta is named for the jet stream, one of VW's wind-themed names, and it is basically a Golf with a trunk.
Volkswagen models.Tiguan: Tiguan's name came from a reader contest and blends the German words for tiger and iguana.
Volkswagen models.Touareg: The Touareg is named for the Tuareg nomads of the Sahara, and it shares its underpinnings with the Porsche Cayenne.
Volkswagen models.Up: The Up is VW's tiny city car, launched in 2011, and its name is written with an exclamation mark in some markets.
Volkswagen models.Scirocco: The Scirocco is named for a hot Mediterranean wind, and Italian designer Giorgetto Giugiaro styled the original.
Volkswagen models.Arteon: The Arteon is VW's sleek fastback, introduced in 2017 as the successor to the Passat CC.
Volkswagen models.Fiesta: The Fiesta is Ford's small car, a Volkswagen rival for decades.
Volkswagen models.Clio: The Clio is Renault's small hatchback, and it has been a European best-seller since 1990.
Volkswagen models.Corsa: The Corsa is Vauxhall and Opel's supermini, not VW's, and it is among Britain's best-sellers.
Volkswagen models.Civic: The Civic is Honda's, and it shares nothing with Volkswagen.
Volkswagen models.Corolla: The Corolla is Toyota's, and it is a rival of the Golf, not a Volkswagen.
Volkswagen models.Micra: The Micra is Nissan's small car, and its first version arrived in 1982.
Volkswagen models.Punto: The Punto is Fiat's supermini, named for the Italian word for point or dot.
Volkswagen models.Yaris: The Yaris is Toyota's small car, and it is a rival to the Polo.
Volkswagen models.Astra: The Astra is Opel and Vauxhall's Golf rival, and its name comes from the Latin for 'star'.
Volkswagen models.A4: The A4 is an Audi. Audi is owned by Volkswagen Group, but it is a separate brand, so it isn't a VW model.
Volkswagen models.Octavia: The Octavia is Skoda's best-seller. Skoda belongs to the VW Group, but it is a separate brand with its own cars.
Volkswagen models.Ibiza: The Ibiza is a SEAT, and SEAT is a Spanish brand owned by the VW Group but sold under its own name.
Volkswagen models.Megane: The Megane is Renault's family hatchback, so it is not a Volkswagen.
Volkswagen models.Mustang: The Mustang is Ford's pony car, which fits Ford, not Volkswagen.

Architectural styles.Gothic: Pointed arches and flying buttresses let Gothic builders raise stone walls full of stained glass; Notre-Dame is a classic.
Architectural styles.Baroque: Born in 17th-century Rome, Baroque used drama, swirling curves and gilded decor to awe churchgoers.
Architectural styles.Art Deco: The Chrysler Building's stainless-steel spire is a peak of Art Deco, a style of geometric glamor from the 1920s.
Architectural styles.Brutalist: The name comes from the French béton brut, 'raw concrete', and not from brutality, whatever critics say.
Architectural styles.Bauhaus: The German Bauhaus school, founded in 1919, taught that form follows function, and shaped modern furniture and design.
Architectural styles.Victorian: Named for Queen Victoria's reign (1837 to 1901), it covers fussy ornament, bay windows and steep gables.
Architectural styles.Tudor: Half-timbered black-and-white houses with steep roofs recall England's Tudor era, though many were built centuries later.
Architectural styles.Romanesque: Thick walls and round arches mark Romanesque, the style that came before Gothic and often looks like a fortress.
Architectural styles.Neoclassical: Neoclassical revived Greek and Roman columns and pediments; the US Capitol and White House follow it.
Architectural styles.Georgian: Georgian houses, named for four King Georges, favor symmetry, sash windows and plain brick fronts.
Architectural styles.Modernist: Modernist architects like Mies and Le Corbusier stripped away ornament in favor of glass, steel and open plans.
Architectural styles.Art Nouveau: Art Nouveau twisted plants and flowing lines into ironwork, like the entrances of the Paris Métro stations.
Architectural styles.Rococo: A lighter, frothier offshoot of Baroque, Rococo loved pastels, shells and swirls, and flourished in 18th-century France.
Architectural styles.Impressionism: Impressionism is a painting movement, named after Monet's 'Impression, Sunrise', not a building style.
Architectural styles.Pointillism: Seurat built images from tiny dots of color, a painting technique, not architecture.
Architectural styles.Fauvism: Critics called Matisse's circle 'fauves', or wild beasts, for their bold colors, in a painting movement of 1905.
Architectural styles.Dadaism: Dada was an anti-art movement born in Zurich in 1916 during the First World War.
Architectural styles.Pop Art: Pop Art took ads and comics as its subject, and Warhol's soup cans made it famous, but it's an art style, not a building one.
Architectural styles.Haiku: A haiku is a Japanese poem, traditionally 5-7-5 syllables, and has nothing to do with buildings.
Architectural styles.Sonnet: A sonnet has 14 lines, a form Shakespeare used 154 times, so it fits poetry, not blueprints.
Architectural styles.Tango: The tango is a dance from Buenos Aires and Montevideo, and the letter T in the NATO alphabet.
Architectural styles.Waltz: The waltz, in three-quarter time, once scandalized Europe because couples held each other so close.
Architectural styles.Limerick: A limerick is a five-line comic poem, and Limerick is also an Irish city, but neither is an architectural style.
Architectural styles.Ballad: A ballad tells a story in verse or song, so it belongs with poetry and music, not buildings.

Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Shamrock: Legend says St Patrick used its three leaves to explain the Trinity; Ireland's emblem is the three-leaf clover.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Leprechaun: Folklore's shoemaker fairy who guards a pot of gold; the name probably derives from Irish for 'small body'.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Guinness: Arthur Guinness signed a 9,000-year lease on the St James's Gate brewery in Dublin in 1759, at 45 pounds a year.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Blarney Stone: Kissing it near Cork is said to grant eloquence; visitors lean backwards over a drop to reach it.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Claddagh: The ring shows hands holding a crowned heart for friendship, love and loyalty; it comes from a fishing village near Galway.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Shillelagh: A knobbly blackthorn or oak club used as a walking stick and weapon, named for a village in County Wicklow.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Dublin: Ireland's capital, whose name comes from the Irish 'dubh linn', meaning black pool.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Soda bread: Made with baking soda instead of yeast, so it needs no rising; a cross cut on top was said to let the fairies out.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Riverdance: It began as a seven-minute interval act at the 1994 Eurovision Song Contest in Dublin, then became a worldwide hit.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Giant's Causeway: About 40,000 interlocking basalt columns on the Antrim coast formed in volcanic activity; legend credits the giant Finn McCool.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Cliffs of Moher: Rising to about 214 meters above the Atlantic in County Clare, they appear in Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Book of Kells: A lavishly decorated Gospel manuscript made around the year 800, kept at Trinity College Dublin.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Kilt: Scottish Highland dress, not Irish; modern Irish kilts exist, but the garment is tied to Scotland.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Haggis: Scotland's dish of sheep's offal, oats and spices, celebrated on Burns Night every January 25.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Loch Ness: A Scottish lake, home of the supposed monster, that holds more fresh water than all the lakes of England and Wales together.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Thistle: Scotland's national emblem; legend says its prickles saved a sleeping Scottish camp from barefoot Norse raiders.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Daffodil: Wales's national flower, worn on St David's Day; Wales also uses the leek, perhaps because their Welsh names are alike.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Tartan: A woven check pattern tied to Scottish clans, with thousands of registered designs.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Edinburgh: Scotland's capital, whose castle sits on an extinct volcano and whose August festivals make up the world's largest arts festival.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Cardiff: Wales's capital, which only became the official capital in 1955.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Welsh dragon: Y Ddraig Goch, the red dragon on the Welsh flag, linked in legend to Merlin's prophecy.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Stonehenge: An English Neolithic monument in Wiltshire, begun about 5,000 years ago; some of its bluestones came from Wales.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Big Ben: Strictly the bell inside the Elizabeth Tower in London, not the clock or tower; it is English, not Irish.
Irish things (not Scottish or Welsh).Highland games: Scottish gatherings with caber tossing, piping and hammer throws, whose roots go back centuries.
